articles.title: Pope Leo names Gerry Delos Reyes as Jolo apostolic vicar
articles.summary: A ,issionary priest who served in Thailand has been named Jolo's new vicar.

blocks.text: November 22, 2026 | 10:25am

Bishop-elect Gerry Gamaliel Sebastian Delos Reyes, who is the current provincial superior of the Congregation of Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate in the Philippines, who is appointed by Pope Leo XIV as the Apostolic Vicar of Jolo.
OMI WORLD
MANILA, Philippines — Pope Leo XIV has appointed a Filipino missionary priest and provincial superior as the new apostolic vicar of Jolo, Sulu.

In a statement on Saturday, November 21 (Vatican time), the Holy See Press Office announced the appointment of Rev. Gerry Gamaliel Sebastian Delos Reyes, provincial superior of the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate (OMI) in the Philippines.
He succeeds Charlie Inzon, who was appointed archbishop of Cotabato in September 2025.

According to the Vatican, Delos Reyes was born on August 14, 1964, in Cotabato City. He studied philosophy at Notre Dame University in Cotabato City and theology at the Loyola School of Theology in Quezon City.
He professed his perpetual vows on September 14, 1989, and was ordained a priest on April 24, 1993.
Early in his ministry, he served as parish priest of Our Lady of Salvation Parish in Timanan from 1993 to 1996 and as parish vicar of Our Lady of Grace Parish in Caloocan City from 1996 to 1998.

Missionary work. After studying the Thai language from 1998 to 2000, he served as parish priest of Saint Clement Mary Hofbauer Parish in the Diocese of Udonthani, Thailand, from 2000 to 2003, and Christ the King Parish in Loei from 2012 to 2014.

He also held several formation and leadership posts in Thailand, serving as superior of the post-novitiate from 2003 to 2006, assistant to the superior of the postulancy from 2006 to 2008, and superior of the juniorate from 2008 to 2012.
Delos Reyes also served as fourth counselor of the Thai-Lao Delegation from 2004 to 2007, first counselor from 2007 to 2013, and eventually its superior from 2013 to 2019.
He was appointed provincial superior of the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate in the Philippines in 2020.

articles.title: Comelec sees 4M new voters for 2028 polls; sets Sept 2027 for COC filing
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Sunday is expecting an additional four million registered voters for the 2028 national and local elections (NLE), as it set the filing of certificates of…

blocks.text: Published November 22, 2026 10:18am

The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Sunday is expecting an additional four million registered voters for the 2028 national and local elections (NLE), as it set the filing of certificates of candidacy (COCs) from September 20 to 26, 2027.

“Mga three million ang target natin [sa voter registration]. Pero sa sobrang laki ng mga nagpaparehistro bawat araw… baka abutin pa tayo ng apat na milyon,” Comelec chairperson George Garcia told Super Radyo dzBB.
(Our target for voter registration is around three million. But given the huge number of people registering every day, we may reach as many as four million.)
“Sa kasalukuyan, mga 140,000 to 150,000 na ang nagparehistro simula November 10,” he added.
(As of now, around 140,000 to 150,000 people have registered since November 10.)
Comelec has scheduled the voter registration from November 10, 2026 to July 30, 2027.
Earlier this month, Comelec urged eligible voters to register early and to take advantage of the long voter registration period rather than wait to do it at the last minute.
2028 polls to proceed
Garcia reiterated that the 2028 NLE would push through, saying it would be “impossible” to postpone it since it is mandated by the 1987 Philippine Constitution.
“100% namin ginagarantiya sa sambayanan na may halalan po tayo para sa 2028 (We 100% guarantee that we will have the election in 2028),” Garcia said.
He added that preparations for the 2028 elections are underway, with Comelec set to begin procuring at least 135,000 vote-counting machines for 2028 polls.
Almost P23 billion was allocated for the procurement of the machines that will be leased for the 2028 polls. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Rains to persist in parts of Luzon, Mindanao through midweek
articles.summary: Easterlies are forecast to become the dominant weather system by Thursday and Friday.

blocks.text: Weather
November 22, 2026 | 10:09am

A shear line is a narrow zone where there is an abrupt change in the horizontal wind component parallel to this line. In the Philippines, it's often associated with the northeast monsoon (amihan) season.

MANILA, Philippines — Parts of northern and eastern Luzon and Mindanao may continue to experience rains through the middle of the week before easterlies become the dominant weather system nationwide by Thursday, state weather bureau PAGASA said.
For Sunday and Monday, November 22 to 23, the shear line is forecast to bring cloudy skies with scattered rains and isolated thunderstorms over Cagayan Valley and Aurora.
Eastern and Central Visayas may also experience scattered rains and thunderstorms due to easterlies.
The intertropical convergence zone, meanwhile, is likely to bring similar conditions over Northern Mindanao, SOCCSKSARGEN, Caraga, Davao Region and Palawan.
Ilocos Region and the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region may have isolated light rains due to the northeast monsoon or amihan.
The rest of the country, including Metro Manila, may expect partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms.
PAGASA's 4 a.m. forecast for Sunday warned of possible flash floods or landslides due to moderate to heavy rains over mainland Cagayan, Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya, Quirino and Aurora.
Similar hazards are possible over Caraga, Davao Region and Southern Leyte due to moderate to at times heavy rains from the ITCZ.
Rains continue through Wednesday
From Tuesday to Wednesday, November 24 to 25, amihan is forecast to bring cloudy skies with rains over Batanes and the Babuyan Islands.
The shear line will continue to affect Aurora and the rest of Cagayan Valley, where scattered rains and isolated thunderstorms are expected.
Most of Mindanao may also remain mostly cloudy with scattered rains and thunderstorms due to the ITCZ.

Metro Manila and the rest of the country are forecast to have partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms, particularly over the eastern sections of Southern Luzon and the Visayas.
Easterlies to dominate by Thursday
By Thursday and Friday, November 26 to 27, easterlies are expected to become the dominant weather system across the country.
PAGASA said generally partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms may be expected, mostly in the afternoon or evening.
The weather bureau said its weekly outlook may still be updated if significant changes develop in its succeeding 24-hour forecasts and advisories.

articles.title: Victorian Greens seek urgent injunction over how-to-vote cards mimicking party’s branding but preferencing it last
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s cards instruct people to vote in a way that would benefit Liberal party

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Victorian Greens have won a supreme court injunction to stop an independent candidate from handing out how to vote cards that mimic their branding and urge people to preference it last.

The decision has been welcomed by the party’s leader, Ellen Sandell, who said the flyers distributed by people wearing the exact same colour shirts as genuine Greens volunteers had already misled voters.
“The last thing people need when they walk into a polling booth is dodgy how-to-vote material designed to trick them into voting the exact opposite way they intended,” Sandell said.
The decision comes after Guardian Australia confirmed that people handing out material for the independent candidate, Tosh-Jake Finnigan, were initially offered $25 an hour to do so.

As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

The card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

The Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.
Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.

blocks.caption: A now destroyed how-to-vote card distributed by Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign at prepoll on Wednesday morning.

blocks.text: “Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card said.
But the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. He told the court the flyers were designed to mislead voters.

“There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth said.
Guardian Australia has confirmed an ad on Airtasker offering payment to those handing out flyers at pre-poll in Prahran was for Finnegan’s campaign.
“I need people to hand out flyers at election booths in Prahran and Richmond $25 per hour during the day from 18-28 November,” the ad said.
But the person who published the ad, Finnegan’s friend Dean Hurston, said no one was recruited through Airtasker as Finnegan had found volunteers elsewhere.
Justice John Watson granted the injunction on both how-to-vote cards on Sunday morning, after hearing testimony from the Victorian Electoral Commission on Saturday afternoon.

Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to quickly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.
“It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said.
Finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print new cards. They said their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.
“I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said.
“The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”
On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.
A decision on whether to grant an injunction will be made on Sunday morning.
Finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.
The former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

articles.title: How one teen turns internet trends into viral Filipino covers
articles.summary: After listeners mistook his recordings for AI-generated music, young TikTok creator Malin — whose hit covers include 'Seis Syete' and 'Made in Philippines' — makes it clear that every lyric and note…

blocks.text: The question kept appearing under Malin’s videos: Was the voice real, or had it been generated by artificial intelligence (AI)?
After viewers began mistaking his covers for AI-generated music, the 16-year-old TikTok creator added a blunt line to his bio: “NO AI USE HERE.”

Malin, who posts as @postju on TikTok, said the questions started after someone posted one of his covers with its lyrics. Viewers assumed the recording was made by AI, and his own comment section soon filled with people asking the same thing.
The reaction was frustrating, he said. But it also pushed him to make clear that his covers were made by a person, not a machine.

As of November 20, 2026, Malin’s TikTok account had about 32,300 followers. Three of his most-viewed Filipino covers — “Seis Syete,” “Made in Philippines” and “Malaki Ka Na” — had reached about 3.7 million, 2.4 million, and 1.3 million views, respectively.
Music has always been a way for Malin to express what he feels. He found a community of fellow music fans online and discovered the joy of sharing songs with others.
That community encouraged him to start singing and eventually put his own voice and language into the music he loved, he said.

Malin began posting music covers on TikTok in September 2025, starting with K-pop songs. He enjoyed the challenge of singing in another language, which he described as a stepping stone to exploring his potential.

He also listens to older Original Pilipino Music (OPM) acts such as Cinderella, although he said he does not have any prominent musical influences. His creativity and passion, he added, are what drive him.

The decision to translate songs into Filipino came from his appreciation of the language. “When a song is translated into Filipino, it sounds more intimate and more romantic, like it’s closer to the heart,” he told Rappler.

His shift came after he wrote “Made in Philippines,” a Filipino version of “Made in Japan” by American singer Buck Owens, as a birthday gift for a friend. At the time, his videos usually received about 100 likes in a day. The cover reached 2,000 likes within 24 hours, then continued to gain attention.
That response made him realize that translating songs could become the focus of his content — work he enjoyed doing even before it drew a larger audience.

Malin is among Filipino creators who turn familiar online material into music. DJ Cupcakes makes remixes from viral clips and Filipino internet culture, while music scorer Ralph Novero turns classic Filipino recipes into song covers.
Malin’s choices are often shaped by the trends circulating in his online circles. When looking for songs to cover, he checks with friends and pays attention to the sounds they keep using.
But he does not simply translate lyrics word for word. Instead, he builds his versions around a song’s central theme and the feeling he wants to convey.
“I’d rather capture the feelings than copy the words,” he said.
Most of his covers are serious, but some are satirical and meant to make viewers laugh because of their absurdity. His “Seis Syete” cover, he said, made people both angry and amused.

He often posts a short version first, using a song’s catchiest or most popular section to see whether viewers want more. Malin said TikTok’s copyright system makes it difficult for some longer covers to remain online, so he waits for audience demand before attempting a full version.

Viewers also influence how he posts. Their support encouraged him to upload daily, and he began posting earlier so people could see his videos sooner. He reads comments when he can, taking note of song suggestions and ways to improve his singing and translations.

One comment stayed with him: a listener asked for a full version after the fan’s mother liked Malin’s cover so much that she preferred it to the original. The response changed how he viewed his work. He had thought his covers were low-quality and did not deserve the attention they received.

Despite the growing audience, Malin does not treat his covers as a source of income. He said it would be nice to earn passive income someday, but he is not actively pursuing it. “I’m not doing this for money,” he said.

Malin said making music without AI is a matter of honesty. “Every mistake I make and every note I sing comes from my own effort, my own feelings, and my own voice,” he said. “The human touch is what gives music its soul, and that is something I want to keep.”
He writes lyrics in his Notes app and records using a PC, a Shure SM58 microphone, and a Maono PS22 Lite audio interface. He uses BandLab and FL Studio in his creative process.

He would not want AI to do any part of his covers, especially the singing. Asked whether he would consider using AI as a creative aid, he said no, calling it “lazy” and saying it would make the music “soulless.”
Malin’s experience comes as AI-generated song covers spread on TikTok, prompting artists to raise concerns about job security and the lack of regulation.

Malin said the issue is also about how listeners recognize the work that goes into a song. He hopes to release an original song someday, building on what he has learned from translating and recording covers.
Until then, he continues to make his covers “with all my love and soul” and wants people to remember that the voice they hear is his. – Rappler.com
Dominique Astucia is a Rappler intern studying BA Journalism at the University of Santo Tomas.

articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte slammed the Philippine National Police (PNP) on Saturday, claiming the organization has become "the enforcement arm of politicians."

blocks.text: Published November 22, 2026 9:51am
Vice President Sara Duterte slammed the Philippine National Police (PNP) on Saturday, claiming the organization has become "the enforcement arm of politicians."

"It would be in the best interest of the Philippine National Police (PNP), as an institution, for its Chief to refrain from paying lip service to the claim that the organization is apolitical—a claim that virtually every Filipino knows to be untrue. The PNP, in practice, has become the enforcement arm of politicians," said Duterte in a statement.
Duterte made the claim after the PNP earlier said that there was "no rescue or release" of a former household staff member of the Vice President and four other individuals.
The PNP pointed out that the concerned former staff members of Duterte were not being held captive when police accompanied their lawyers to a hotel in Taguig City on November 17.
However, Duterte pointed out that the PNP did not conduct the proper inquiry on the matter.
"Such a premature conclusion, reached without first establishing the facts, raises serious concerns about the institution’s impartiality and its commitment to due process," Duterte said.

Further, the Vice President said that she has five "documented threats" made by police against her. Yet, she cannot present the threats amid her impeachment trial "because the prosecution maliciously withdrew the charge of grave threats."
Duterte also reiterated that she is concerned for her personal safety.

"When I say that I do not feel safe in this country, I speak not only for myself but also for the many Filipinos who have experienced, or fear experiencing, the failure of law enforcement to make this country a place where people can live with the assurance that their fundamental rights will be respected," she said.
The PNP earlier said that they have yet to report any threat against Duterte and her family when she first made her statement.
GMA News Online reached out to the PNP for a comment on Duterte's latest pronouncements. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Love at first bite: The Paltok bakery that sells out early
articles.summary: Residents of Paltok, Quezon City, flock to a yellow-walled corner bakery every day before its freshly baked bread sells out

blocks.text: Carmen Mariano, 65, used to wonder why so little bread remained whenever she passed by the small bakery in her neighborhood in Barangay Paltok, Quezon City.

It’s called Bong & Dynah Bakeshop, but residents have taken to calling it Matias Bakery, a nod to the street where it’s located. The small shop opens at 5 am to serve classic baked goods to early risers, and for the longest time, Carmen thought the bakery simply offered an oddly tiny selection of bread.
“Anong klaseng bakery ba ‘to? (What kind of bakery is this?)” Carmen would often say to herself whenever she laid her eyes on the big glass case situated in front of the store.
It turned out, however, that by the time she would arrive at the bakeshop, most of them had just already been bought by other customers who happened to get there before she did.
Carmen is now a regular at the bakeshop — making the trip for buns, banana cake, and egg pie. Her son also buys pandesal in the morning.

When Bong & Dynah Bakeshop opens its doors at the crack of dawn, its staff only has a window of one to two hours to enjoy the lull before the morning rush starts. Hordes of customers start pouring in by 6 or 7 am, and by 8 or 9 am, its pandesal is completely sold out.
Spanish bread and pan de coco are among the bakery’s bestsellers, said Dynah Carizal, who owns the shop with her husband Cornellio “Bong” Carizal.

blocks.caption: Spanish bread, pan de coco, and pastries at Bong & Dynah Bakeshop.

blocks.text: This is already Dynah’s second bakery. After spending 10 years as a call center agent, she saved up enough to try her hand at a pastry business again with Bong. Now, the shop is a year old and counting.
The space used to house tapsilog, lugaw, pancit, and fried chicken businesses, until it turned itself into a yellow-walled bakery that residents have quickly come to love.
Bong said their immediate goal is to keep serving customers and keep the business afloat.
“Kami, kumbaga, dahan-dahan lang. Basta magsurvive tayo,” he said.
(We’re taking it slowly. We just want to survive.)

More than just survival, Bong & Dynah Bakeshop has now become a familiar stop despite surrounding businesses coming and going. It’s a staple that looks like it’s here to stay, so long as the people of Paltok keep their love for pastries alive.

Dynah said customers often overlook the time needed for dough to rise, which takes about five to six hours to complete. Bong said that a second batch of the famous salt bread could be ready only after the morning demand dies down.

Making bread is a labor of love that takes more than just mixing ingredients and sticking the dough in the oven. This is something baker Genesis Ordano, who has been working at the shop for 16 years, knows full well.

blocks.caption: Empty shelves show the sold-out putok/star bread. The shop also offers toasted siopao for P15.

blocks.text: Genesis said getting the mixture right takes work customers rarely see. Production uses two and a half sacks of flour, rising to three when sales are good. Like clockwork, the longtime baker — who attests that nothing about the practice of baking challenges him — can recite the whole process of preparing pandesal off the top of his head.
“Magtitimbang muna ng asukal, tapos lalagyan ng asin at mantika. Tapos hahaluin at paalsahin muna. Tapos puputulin,” he explained.
(You weigh the sugar first, then you add salt and oil. Then, you mix it all and let it rise. Then, you cut the dough up.)

Some bread, however, sometimes goes unsold. Still, nothing goes to waste at Bong & Dynah Bakeshop. Genesis said leftovers become crumbs for pudding and custard, while Bong himself also turns some into toast with butter and sugar.

blocks.caption: P50 custard cakes made from leftover bread.

blocks.text: Bong attests that it’s the workers that keep the bakery alive.

While the bakers keep the pastries flowing, saleswoman Joanne keeps the shop running in her own way. Once she clocks in at 6:30 am, she immediately cleans the racks and sweeps up the entire space. Then, she arranges the trays and sets up the tongs and plastic bags used to pack the bread customers will buy.
Joanne, though, has a more difficult task that onlookers may not usually see.

When the demand at the bakery gets high, the challenge of keeping up with it doesn’t only depend on the bakers. It’s a burden Joanne has to bear, too. Sometimes, customers get upset when certain products sell out, but she gets through it all with patience.
“[Kailangan] habaan talaga ang pasensya. Kahit galit ka na, nakangiti ka rin,” she said.
(You really have to be patient. Even when you’re already angry, you still have to smile.)

But at the end of the day, the famed Paltok bakery turns into a home for its employees, many of whom hail from provinces like Iloilo. It provides workers with food and accommodation, and often celebrates their birthdays with meals at places like Mang Inasal.
Shelves may empty by mid-morning, but keeping the bakery going starts before its doors open.

Beyond the loyal customers who buy out the bakery’s bread every single day, the staff is a big contributor to Bong & Dynah Bakeshop’s success, even though the shop is only a year old. Perhaps Bong and Dynah, then, have found the formula to fulfilling their dream of making the bakery survive. – Rappler.com
Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

articles.title: Prosecution asks ICC chamber to reject Rodrigo Duterte defense request on evidence
articles.summary: Prosecutors asked the International Criminal Court Trial Chamber III to dismiss a request of former president Rodrigo Duterte's defense team regarding evidentiary matters as they are procedurally…

blocks.text: Published November 22, 2026 9:04am

Prosecutors asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Pre-Trial Chamber III to dismiss a request of former president Rodrigo Duterte's defense team regarding evidentiary matters as they are procedurally improper.
In a public redacted document released November 20, the prosecutors argued that the defense's request contravenes the chamber's protocols on evidence.

"The Defence’s request to [REDACTED] goes well beyond the scope of the requested observations from the Chamber, namely, [REDACTED]. It also contravenes the Rules of Procedure and Evidence (the 'Rules') and the protocol established by the Chamber regarding challenges to the admissibility of evidence," the document read.

"While the Defence is clearly keen to [REDACTED], the Chamber has established a protocol regarding the submission of evidence, in accordance with rule 64(1) of the Rules, which requires that the parties 'raise issues as to admissibility of evidence, including on any of the standard evidentiary criteria, at the time when the evidence is submitted to the Chamber'," it added.
The prosecution added that the defense should raise its alleged concerns when the Prosecution actually submits the relevant evidence, rather than improperly couching its request inside observations.
"The Defence may therefore raise its alleged concerns [REDACTED] when it is submitted by the Prosecution instead of improperly couching the request in observations related to [REDACTED]," it said.
Moreover, the prosecutors also sought to correct a factual error made by the defense regarding specific statements central to the ongoing proceedings.

"The Prosecution also wishes to correct a mistaken submission made by the Defence. The Defence argues that [REDACTED]. However, the [REDACTED] at issue in these proceedings. The [REDACTED].[REDACTED].It is the [REDACTED]. Although [REDACTED]. The statements made by [REDACTED] at issue in these proceedings," the document further read.
The prosecutors' comments were submitted before Trial Chamber III judges Joanna Korner, Keebong Paek, and Nicolas Guillou.
The defense recently asked the chamber to reject the testimony of an ex-Davao City police officer, according to a public redacted filing released on November 18.

Duterte’s counsel Peter Haynes contested the admission of P-0002’s evidence, saying the articles invoked by the Office of the Prosecutor to collect and preserve it require proof that a witness can no longer testify orally.
“Absent such proof, the prior recorded testimony cannot be admitted and the witness must be called to give his evidence viva voce,” Haynes said.
The trial of Duterte for crimes against humanity will open on November 30, with judges first asking him whether he admits guilt or pleads not guilty.
The hearing will begin at 10 a.m. in The Hague (5 p.m. Philippine time).
The chamber earlier found Duterte fit to stand trial, stating that he “is able to effectively exercise his fair trial rights in the proceedings.”

Duterte was arrested in March 2025 at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3 and is currently detained at the ICC Detention Centre in Scheveningen in The Hague, The Netherlands. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: ‘No time for a culture war’: Victoria’s electricity supply is at risk. Can it avoid power shortages and bill shocks?
articles.summary: State faces electricity supply gap when Yallourn coal-fired power station closes in 2028 as experts warn neither Labor nor the Coalition has adequate plans

blocks.text: Victoria’s electricity supply will be at risk when a major power plant shuts in 2028 and neither major party is offering a plan at this month’s state election to deal with it, experts have warned.

All parties concede the giant Yallourn coal plant, which has operated in the Latrobe Valley since the 1970s and supplies a fifth of Victoria’s energy, is at the end of its functional life and will shut in less than two years. Analysts say the parties vying to run the state are failing to properly explain how they will fill the power shortfall the closure will create.

The challenge facing Victoria is exacerbated by the growth in energy demand from datacentres and the electrification of buildings, homes and vehicles. Experts are most critical of the Coalition, under Liberal leader Jess Wilson, which is favoured to win the election. It says it would stop work on new transmission lines – the high-voltage power lines needed to connect new wind and solar farms and allow Victoria to import power from neighbouring states.

Tim Baxter, of consultancy Naru Research, says there is no “time for a culture war on energy in Victoria” because poor choices now would be “devastating” for the state’s economy and create bill shocks for households and businesses.

He says cheap gas helped build Victoria’s past prosperity, but it is quickly running out with offshore gas supply from Bass Strait in steep decline. And there is no evidence the state has meaningful gas resources elsewhere to replace it. This has contributed to a 62% increase in gas prices in five years, he says, while electricity bills have risen by 18%.

Given Victorians rely more on gas than other states, Baxter says it underlines the need for households to move away from gas and increasingly run on renewable energy. “Every windfarm, solar farm and battery that comes online before 2028 reduces how much expensive gas Victoria has to burn when Yallourn goes. That makes speeding up the build-out the single best way to protect households from higher bills,” he says.
What are Labor and the Coalition promising?

Victoria’s wholesale electricity prices are the lowest on the east coast, but households still rely heavily on expensive gas. Regardless of who wins, energy bills are likely to increase, according to a government briefing reported in the Herald Sun.

The Coalition says it would scrap VNI West, a transmission line linking Victoria to New South Wales, and pause work on the Western Renewables Link, between Melbourne and the state’s west. Instead, it would undertake a “short, sharp and independent” review of the state’s transmission plan, which would consider alternatives, such as solar power on commercial and industrial rooftops.

It has also pledged to “throw open the doors to gas exploration”, reverse Labor’s policy of making new homes all-electric, and tender for new firming capacity with an Energy Security Requirement modelled on schemes in NSW and South Australia. There is no plan to change the state’s emission reduction targets – cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 75%–80% below 2005 levels by 2035 and reaching net zero emissions by 2045 – but it has not said how it would achieve them.

Labor says it would continue to expand the power grid, shift homes from gas to electricity for heating and cooking and continue to support the development of offshore windfarms. But the Carroll government is also reviewing the Western Renewables Link. It recently cancelled a renewable energy zone, approved two gas developments (although one has since entered administration), and announced $7.5m to kickstart a “renewable gas industry”.

Nexa Advisory chief executive Stephanie Bashir says new transmission is crucial for developing renewable energy and allowing power to be imported across state lines at times of high demand, such as during heatwaves. “This is not the time to be cancelling any of the projects in the pipeline,” she says. “This is the time where we put our foot on the accelerator and go hard.”

Environment Victoria’s chief executive, Jono La Nauze, says the Coalition’s plan – including a proposal to reinstate a policy introduced by the previous Baillieu-Napthine Coalition government preventing wind turbines being built within 2km of dwellings – is “the greatest swindle ever attempted on Victorian voters”.

“The Coalition are promising to stop all the things that are necessary to replace our coal and gas generation. They’ve got some quick slogans for how they’re going to instead rely on gas, with absolutely no substance,” he says.
But analysts say Labor is also not building energy infrastructure fast enough.
after newsletter promotion
Oliver Nunn, managing director of the consultancy Endgame Analytics, says the lack of an adequate plan to stave off an energy shortfall means that “whoever wins [the election], we lose”.
“You can see demand for electricity pulling up rapidly in Victoria, 5% year-on-year growth,” Nunn says. “Coal’s going out, and we just do not have, at this point, a really viable plan.”

blocks.caption: The Golden Plains windfarm in Victoria’s central highlands. Labor plans to finalise the state’s first auction for offshore wind power. Photograph: Stuart Walmsley/The Guardian

blocks.text: In its 12 years in government, Labor has overseen a surge in Victoria’s share of renewable energy from 10% to 44% and the closure of the large Hazelwood coal-fired power station. The number of windfarms has grown from 14 to 44 and large-scale solar farms from two to 57. Labor also ended the state’s moratorium on conventional gas exploration in 2021.
But the state’s auditor general says both VNI West and the Western Renewables Link are behind schedule, and not likely to be completed until after Yallourn’s scheduled close.

Recent attempts to fast-track the process by legislating for compulsory land acquisition before environmental approvals have been unpopular in regional communities, but Labor says the changes were needed to reduce delays and improve certainty for landowners. Controversially, Labor also passed laws to allow VicGrid and its contractors access to private land without a landholder’s consent, as a last resort to facilitate works.

“Every time the government seems to hit a hurdle, what they’ve done is not gone back and reassessed the engagement and tried to improve it, what they’ve done is changed legislation to give them broader powers,” the Victorian Farmers Federation president, Ryan Milgate, says.
The shadow energy minister, David Davis, refers to the laws as Labor’s “double bazooka powers” and says the Coalition will ditch them and reinstate landholder appeal rights.
But Nexa’s Bashir says energy policy should not be “a political football”.
“We do need to back the replacement generation. We can’t do any more reviews; we’ve just got to get on with it.”

articles.title: [Tambay] Paasa pa rin ang depensa ni VP Sara
articles.summary: Nangako ang mga abogado ni Vice President Sara Duterte na mayroon silang mga pasabog na testigo. Hanggang ngayon, nganga pa rin ako.

blocks.text: “There are no accidents.”
Ang linyang iyan ay isa sa mga paborito ng inyong friendly neighborhood tambay. Isa ito sa mga siping sinabi ni Master Oogway, ang pawikang maéstro sa maalamát na pelikulang Kung Fu Panda.

Ang ibig sabihin ng pantas ay laging may dahilan ang báwat pangyayari, at hindi bastá-bastá nangyayari ito. Walang aksidente o walang nagkakataon lang. May paliwanag kaya nagkakilala kayo. May dahilán ang pagsasalubong ng inyong landas. Pinagtatagpo ang lahat ng pangyayari, hindi ito “good timing” lang. Hindi ala-suwérte ang “being in the right place at the right time.”

At noong Biyernes, Nobyembre 19, pumasok sa isip ng inyong tambay na, bagamá’t hindi raw sinasadya, may dahilan kung bakit may sumiklab na visual effects ng naglalagablab na apoy sa broadcast ng impeachment trial ni Vice President Sara Duterte.

Day 44 ng impeachment (panoorin dito mula sa markang 56:16 minute), tóka ni Senator Alan Peter Cayetano ang opening prayer. Nakapikit at nakayuko pa ang senador. Nakatayo sa rostrum at may bukas na Bibliya sa harap niya. Nakikita ng mga manonood na taimtim na nananalangin ang senador. Bago matapos ang dasal, pagkasabi ni Cayetano ng “make it very, very clear whether a conviction is in order or an acquittal,” saglit na sumikláb at nabalot ang screen ng mga nanonood mula sa kaliwa pakanan ng transition effect ng lumagabláb na apoy.
Ang bilis ng pangyayari. Ano ‘yun? Bahagi ba ‘yun ng pa-effect ng dasal ni Cayetano? Pagkakamali lang ba ng admin ng tech na nangangasiwa ng live stream?

Noong hapon ding iyon, humingi ng paumanhín ang Public Relations and Information Bureau ng Senado. Sabi ng PRIB sa kanilang pahayag: “We sincerely apologize for the accidental transition effect that appeared during the live stream of the Senate Impeachment Court proceedings today.” Ang sinisisi: “[an] unexpected technical issue during the broadcast, which we deeply regret.”

Bumuô agad ng kuwénto ang malikót na utak ng inyong tambay. Siguro dahil palígoy-lígoy ‘yung panalangin, pabirông pumasok sa isip ng isang nasa tech booth ng Senado na “singitan ko kaya ng maapoy na pa-effect” ‘yung eksena ni Cayetano? Káso, nagkatotoo ang iniisip niya nang hindi sinadyâng napindot ang transition button.
Ilang beses na ring nangyari sa inyong tambay iyan. Pabirô lang dapat o kaya’y usapang “atin-atin lang ito, ha” kaso naro-wrong send. Naku po, sabit na naman!

Pinagalitan ni presiding judge Senator Chiz Escudero ang Senate PRIB sa nangyari. Sabi ng senador: “The flames are not well-taken and inappropriate in this proceedings.” Iniútos ni Escudero na alisin ang eksena sa talaan ng Senado.

May mananagot kaya sa PRIB kung hilingin ni Senator Alan na disiplináhin ang may sala? Pero wala akong nabasang komento ni Cayetano sa nangyari. Na-let-go na kaya niya? O baka naman may hindi tayo nalalaman?
Ilang beses na binanggít ng tambay ninyo na, “looking forward” itong marinig ang sagot ng depensa ni Vice President Sara Duterte sa mga ibinibintang sa kanya sa gumugulong na pagdinig.

Noong sinabi ng prosekusyon na tapos na silang ihayag ang mga ebidénsiyá ng kanilang articles of impeachment, sabay isinapubliko pa ang pagbawi sa tatlo sa apat, natuwa ako dahil sa wakas maririnig ko na ang panig ng depensa ni VP Sara. Oras na para ang depensa naman ang maglahad ng kanilang ebidénsiyá. Malalaman na natin ang mga arguménto ni Duterte.
Sabi pa nga ng abogado ni VP Sara na si Michael Poa, may paliwanag sila sa mga ipinukól ng prosekusyon. Dagdag ni atorni, ang mga saksi ng depensa ang tutugon.
Ilang linggo na ang lumipas, ngangá pa rin ako.
Inasahan ng publiko ang matinding balik ng depensa sa mga ibinató sa kanila. Parang may nagsabi pa nga, hindi ko lang maalala kung sino, hintayin daw ang pasabog ng panig ni VP Sara.
Pero puro mintís ang mga testigo ng depensa.
Pinakamabigat na sanang saksi itong ipinakilalang anti-money laundering expert na si Rainer dela Fuente, CPA at abogado.

Sa pag-unawà ko bilang isang hamak na tambay, napiling saksi ng depensa si Dela Fuente para tibagin ang nilalaman ng financial analysis na iniharap bilang ebidensya ng prosekusyon sa impeachment court. Ang financial analysis ay nagsasabi diumanó ng hindi maipaliwanag at nakatagong yaman ni VP Sara.

Sa ulat na isinumité sa impeachment court ng saksi ng prosekusyon na nagpakilalang forensic financial analyst at abogadong si Alex Cabrera, sinabi niya na sa kanyang “conservative estimate” mayroong hindi idineklarang yaman si VP Sara na P817.87-million.

Kahit mas maalam sa anti-money laundering si Dela Fuente, tumestigo siya sa tingin niyang pagkukulang ng financial analysis. Ang problema sa opinyon ng testigo ng depensa ay hindi niya nabasa ang buong financial analysis. Sa huli, sinabi ni atorni na ang mga nasabi niya ay sagot lang niya sa mga theoretical na itinanong sa kanya.
Tanggap ng inyong tambay ang sinabing iyan ng testigo.

Ang hindi ko mapapalampas ay nang usisain ang political affiliation ni Dela Fuente. Nasabi kasi niya sa unang bahagi ng testimonya niya na wala siyang political affiliation. Sa katunayan, hindi siya bumoto noong 2019.

Pero parang nabalatan ang testigo nang tinanong siya ni Senator Kiko Pangilinan tungkol sa kanyang malapit na kaibigan at dating law partner mula 2018 hanggang 2021. ‘Yung law partner ni Dela Fuente ay dating counsel ng Duterte Youth. At sinabi rin ni Pangilinan na ang law partner na iyon ay supporter din ni kandidatong Rodrigo Duterte nung halalan ng 2016. Si Dela Fuente, ‘yung law partner, at si Digong ay kapwa mga nagtapos sa San Beda Law.
Sinabi ni Dela Fuente na hindi niya alam na ang law partner niya ay sumuporta kay Tatay Digong. Hindi rin niya alam na abogado ng Duterte Youth kahit magka-partner sila sa law firm.

Sunod na tanong ni Sen Kiko: “Sabi mo hindi ka bumoto since 2019. Sinong binoto mo noong 2016 presidential election?” Hindi na raw niya maalala, sabi ni atorni. Tinanong pa ni Dela Fuente: “Sino po ba ang kandidato noon?”
Tulad na din ng mga naunang testigo, naging makakalimutin na si atorni.

Gusto ko sanang tanungin si atorni: Kung sakaling maalala mong si Tatay Digong pala ang ibinoto mo noong 2016, kahit ’ika mo nga “ang tagal na nun,” wala namang mali doon. Eh, sa iyon ang kandidatong pinaniwalaan mo.

At nasa mga disclosure din lang naman tayo, inaamin ko na pabor ako kay Tatay Digong noong 2016. Ang paniniwala ko kasi ay panahon na para magkaroon ang Pilipinas ng presidente na taga-Mindanao. Kahit hindi ko siya kilala, dahil taga-Mindanao siya, dapat subukan naman natin.
Malay ko bang magkakaganoon tayo? Sorry na po. – Rappler.com
Si Chito de la Vega ay Tambay ng Rappler dalawang beses kada buwan. Kasama rin siya sa mga anchor-host ng programang Balita Kwento Serbisyo ng DZME 1530.

articles.title: Fred Nile, former NSW politician and figurehead of the rightwing Christian Democratic party, dies aged 92
articles.summary:
Controversial figure frequently took positions against drug use, abortion and homosexuality, but in later years supported legislation expunging homosexual convictions

  • Get our

blocks.text: The former New South Wales MP and longstanding figurehead of the rightwing Christian Democratic party, the Rev Fred Nile, has died aged 92.
Nile was a member of the NSW legislative council for more than 40 years. He first entered the state’s upper house in 1981 and retired after unsuccessfully contesting the 2023 election.

Nile was a controversial figure; a standard-bearer for Christian and social conservative politics since long before the formation of the Australian Christian Lobby and other faith-based political movements.

“It is with deep sadness the Nile family announces the passing of Rev. the Hon. Frederick John Nile who passed away peacefully on the 21st of November at the age of 92,” his family said in a statement.
“Rev. Nile is survived by his wife, children, grandchildren and great grandchildren.
“Details about a service or memorial will be shared soon.”
Nile, an ordained Congregational Union minister, and the political party he led for decades frequently took positions against drug use, abortion and homosexuality.

Alex Greenwich, the member for Sydney, said that despite disagreeing on “a lot” with Nile, the pair had a good working relationship, particularly in relation to protecting First Nations cultural sites.
“Rev. Nile also played a key role in passing legislation for the expungement of prior homosexual convictions, landmark laws that cleared the names of hundreds of gay men,” Greenwich said.

“Rev. Nile played the ball, not the person. His opposition to many of the reforms I delivered came from his faith, and he didn’t engage in the personalised vitriol that comes from many of today’s right-wing politicians.”
after newsletter promotion
Greenwich said he had asked premier Chris Minns for a state funeral for Nile.

Lyle Shelton, who had initially been chosen by Nile as his successor to lead the Christian Democratic Party in 2021 before the pair had a falling out, said Nile “stood in the public square for Christian ethics and moral virtues at time when few would”.
“Cruelly caricatured by his opponents, anyone who met him knew the caricature of the mockers did not fit,” Shelton said.

articles.title: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
articles.summary: Fewer young people have registered to vote in next year's election than in 2023 - are young people losing faith in democracy?

blocks.text: Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.
At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.
He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.
"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.
But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.
Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.
The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.
His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.
Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).
Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.
The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.
In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".
His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.
But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.
"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.
The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.
Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.

But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.
Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobile around political causes.
But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.
Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.
"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.
The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.
Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.
Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.
Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.
This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.
But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.
Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.
"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.
Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.
For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.
Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.
The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.
Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.
The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.

The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; £56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.
Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.
These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.
Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.
The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.
Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.

"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

"Young Nigerians are poor. Nigerian politics is cash-intensive, so participation is guided by money," she says, adding that young people are often content with having a bit of influence as a special advisor to a senior politician.
But political analyst Seun Ajayi believes the problems go beyond the financial barriers.
"We have some of the most brilliant young persons in the world, but they are either not interested in politics or feel satisfied when given a small role in government," he says.
"The old men are not going to sit idle and allow us to push them out. We have to fight for the big positions, but at the moment I don't see the zeal."
Umar believes changing attitudes towards young leadership is equally important.
"Culturally, we are not primed to trust or accept the brilliance of a younger person, so it will be very difficult," she says.
"Old men are still holding on to the system."
Some Nigerians took inspiration from the wave of success of young candidates in the recent midterm elections in the US, some of whom have roots in Africa.
"America Has Done It, Can Nigerians Do the Same?" entertainer Charly Boy wrote on X, in a post that was widely shared.
He said the US results served as a warning to Nigerian politicians that no matter how powerful the political machine, voters can change the direction of government.
He called on young people to interrogate candidates about their past promises: "Has life improved? Where are the jobs, security and affordable living?
"Democracy is not a spectator sport, nor is it about sharing rice," he wrote.

articles.title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
articles.summary: When 16-year-old Landon Tresp met a teenage girl in an online game, it led to him and his mother helping the FBI rescue her from kidnapping.

blocks.text: Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.
She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.

He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.

Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.

That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.
"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.
The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.
Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.

"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".
"She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.
But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.
They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".

After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.
Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.
Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.
During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".
Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".

The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.
"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.
Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.
The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.

Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.
"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.
"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.

When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.
He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.

After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.
The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.
He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.
As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.
While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.
She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.

Law enforcement was "phenomenal…giving me an update, you know, 'We're nine minutes out, we're seven minutes out,'" says Khristina, who was on the phone with Jenny the entire time, her son Landon watching at her side.
Khristina could hear other people in the home with Jenny, and she was afraid that someone would catch wind of what was happening and harm the girl.
But she kept any of those fears from Jenny.

"I want you to take three deep breaths with me," she told the teen. "When an officer tells me to go, and I relay that message to you, I want you to run up those stairs as fast as you can … Grab that basement door.
"I want you to keep going down that hallway and grab that front door… do not stop.'"
The mother and son watched breathlessly as Jenny ran into the arms of a state trooper.

Harmel is now in federal custody and has been charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Local Oregon media also reported he'd been accused of sexually abusing a six-year-old in the months before Jenny disappeared - and a sexual abuse protective order was granted against him in March 2025.
He remains behind bars awaiting trial.
A lawyer for the defendant did not respond to a BBC request for comment.
Jenny, meanwhile, remains in daily communication with Khristina and Landon - who still enjoys playing online games with her.

"Sometimes we just sit on video chat, just so she knows she has someone that cares," Khristina says. "She was on video last night when I cooked dinner …it's nice to know that when she has a bad day or a bad moment, she can call me right away or call Landon right away."
"She's doing great for what she's gone through."
They haven't met in person yet, but they're in the process of trying to make that happen.
"I hope I can put my arms around her soon," Khristina says.

articles.title: Trailblazers in the desert: 5 Filipinos make their mark in Dubai
articles.summary: Whether topping global essay contests or rising from odd jobs to five-star hotel management, these students and professionals highlight the resilience and talent of the Filipino community in the…

blocks.text: DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Five Filipinos, two of them children of overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), are blazing trails in this fast-paced global city.

Three of them — a businesswoman who is the lone Filipino member of a Dubai Chamber of Commerce business group, a high school graduate who earned a degree online to become a hotelier, and a social media specialist working with the Dubai government — all rose from humble beginnings.

The other two, both children of OFWs, are excelling in school. One is a published author — having written a trilogy — with immersion experience at Oxford University and a string of awards to her name; the other placed 11th overall among more than 1,000 competitors at Yale University’s World Scholar’s Cup Tournament of Champions this month.

Seventeen-year-old Izabella Faye Lebig — deputy head of the student council at Cambridge International School Dubai who boasts a long list of achievements — is a silver awardee in the Queen’s Commonwealth Essay Competition, which drew 25,648 global entries from 54 countries.

She also received a “Very High Commendation (Top 1%)” in the law category at the UK-based John Locke Institute’s 2026 Global Essay Competition, which received more than 100,237 entries from 183 countries, according to the institute.
Moreover, Izabella Faye has won law essay-writing contests at Oxford and Cambridge Universities.

She’s the daughter of Dr. Ben Lebig Jr., a financial analyst at the Dubai office of American multinational energy firm Chevron Corp. He, himself, had come far from being a young boy who had to cross two knee-deep rivers and climb a hill just to get to school in Iloilo.

blocks.caption: Izabella Faye Lebig

blocks.text: A published author, Izabella Faye wrote the Alex Hades trilogy, which she described as exploring the “theological side of fantasy… starting off as a fantasy-suspense and morphing into fantasy-action throughout the series.”

“Overall, I consider the Alex Hades trilogy… an experiment and a diary, where readers can see not only the development of the story itself, but also my development as a writer and a kid growing up,” she said.

While considering business, law, or digital marketing as potential career paths, Izabella Faye — who was once featured at the annual Emirates Literature Festival — said writing remains central to her life.
“One [thing] that I know for sure, though, is that writing will always be my thing all throughout; it’s how my mind and soul breathe, and I practically live off it,” she said.
Writing for film is also on her mind.

“One thing I know for absolute certain is I’ve always wanted an opportunity to bring my stories to the big screen, and really getting involved in the production and the making of how it comes to life — it’s something I knew for sure I wanted to take part in even before I started writing,” Izabella Faye said.
Still, she keeps her feet firmly on the ground.

“I aim for the moon, but even if I land among the stars, I’ll feel just as proud. Achievements like these, as my parents always remind me, are just one part of the journey — they are reminders of how far I’ve come, but they’re not the destination,” she said.

Another OFW child making waves is 17-year-old Ocean Thomas Tayo, who — along with teammates Jillian Denise Pilapil, and Sean Ezekiel Cosmiano — traveled to Yale University in Connecticut for the World Scholar’s Cup Tournament of Champions.

“We were excited. We researched deeper… and met up every now and then for active recall and to try our best to soar high,” said Tayo, a 12th grader at The Philippine School Dubai, which is attended mostly by OFW children.
The team placed 11th overall in the global competition, which featured more than 1,000 participants.

The World Scholar’s Cup is an internationally recognized academic competition where individuals and teams debate, write collaboratively, and answer questions based on an annually updated curriculum. Competitors begin in regional rounds and, after passing a point threshold, qualify for global rounds before advancing to the Tournament of Champions at Yale.

blocks.caption: Ocean Thomas Tayo

blocks.text: Earlier, Ocean’s three-member team placed second in the Dubai Global Round, where he also finished third individually out of hundreds of scholars.

“As an Emirati [resident], I feel fulfilled. After hours and days of hard work, it really all paid off after feeling the medals and trophies, but what makes it worth it the most is bringing pride and joy to the UAE,” said Ocean, noting he had “prepared really hard — a bit too hard.”
“During the competition, I was sick the whole time. However, I still conquered and got 13 medals and seven trophies with my team,” Ocean said.

A student-leader, he founded The Pathfinder’s Project at his school, an initiative focused on personal growth, student direction, and leadership development. He was also named champion of the senior category at the Emirates Environmental Group Public Interest School Speaking Contest and won Best Debater in a simulated International Court of Justice competition.

A Filipino businesswoman, who once commuted daily from Bulacan to Far Eastern University (FEU) in Diliman during college, has been named a board member of the Printing and Publishing Business Group (PPBG) under the Dubai Chamber of Commerce (DCC).
“I am proud of having become a member of the board because I’m carrying our flag and I am the youngest as well,” said 42-year-old Michico Lopez Ramos in a mix of English and Filipino.

“Most of those sitting on the board are older because of their huge experience in the market, and all are males. Hence, I’m so flattered. I can keep up at that level with them, knowing that I’m the youngest and probably have a lot to learn.”
“I am so honored, and I know I can’t achieve this without my team supporting me,” she added.

blocks.caption: Michico Lopez Ramos

blocks.text: Ramos arrived in Dubai in 2004, fresh out of college, and landed a job as a sales representative at a mobile phone and IT shop. Three years later, she ventured into opening her own digital marketing business before launching an events and advertising company in 2021.

Today, she is also co-owner of The Global Stories DXB, an online and print magazine, and the Brilliant Training Institute, which is accredited by Dubai’s Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA).

“My main responsibility as a board member is as sales and marketing director overseeing the group’s brand identity, social media mileage, and online presence, including press releases, website, campaigns, and other marketing collateral,” said Ramos, who holds a degree in information technology and an MBA certification in project management.
Ramos said the DCC emailed to ask if she was interested in the position.
“Of course, it involves voting, and I had to share my experience and profile. It was all God’s plan that I was chosen,” she said.

She plans to use her role to “help amplify our voices as Filipinos in the printing and publishing sector.” So far, she has spearheaded the PPBG’s logo and branding guidelines, LinkedIn and Facebook pages, and online member database, among other initiatives.

The PPBG board also includes elected and founding industry representatives such as Secretary General Hamid Maammer, Lakshmanan Ganapathy of Al Ghurair Printing & Publishing, and Roger Nicodeme of Heidelberg Gulf LLC.
Ronin Ronald Endozo of Candelaria, Quezon, went to Oman as a high school graduate at just 16 years old in 1994.
“My first three years… were some of the hardest of my life. With limited experience and skills, I struggled to find my footing and moved from one job to another just to get by,” recalled Endozo.

Now 49 years old and recently appointed general manager of a five-star luxury serviced apartment hotel, Endozo worked his share of odd jobs before pulling himself together, pursuing a college degree at 41, and reaping what he sowed.

“I worked as a garage helper, a car washer in public parking areas, a kiosk attendant, a dishwasher in a coffee shop, a catering assistant, a cargo-moving helper, a bakery helper, a meat shop attendant and cutter, and a food server,” Endozo said.

Born and raised in a remote area, Endozo grew up in a small nipa hut with no electricity, with the nearest water source at least half a kilometer away. He has eight siblings, and his father worked as a carpenter in their barangay.

“Even as a young child, I already understood how hard our life was. We considered ourselves lucky if we could eat three times a day, or if we had any viand to go with our rice. I attended elementary school in our barangay, which meant walking more than a kilometer every morning, then walking back home at noon for lunch, because we couldn’t bring packed meals. Our parents often didn’t even know whether there would be anything for us to eat at midday. Many times, our meal was nothing more than rice and salt,” narrated Endozo .
He finished elementary school having had money to buy something during recess “only a handful of times.”
“I never experienced owning a new school bag; most of the time, I used an old hand-me-down one or even a fishing net,” he added.

blocks.caption: Ronin Ronald Endozo

blocks.text: Despite these hardships, the Endozo siblings became known at their barangay public school for their strong academic performance.
“That academic excellence became my bridge to continuing my education at a high school in the town proper,” he said.

Endozo earned a scholarship to a private high school in the town proper, though getting there was far from easy. Because his parents couldn’t afford the fare, he had to walk at least three kilometers every day just to reach the main road where he could catch a ride.
He owned only two school uniforms throughout high school. “I never had a textbook of my own and relied entirely on books borrowed from the library,” he shared.

“My daily allowance was always just enough to cover my fare to and from school and a small viand to go with the rice I brought from home. For four years, I lived on mongo soup and pancit habhab as viand.”
After graduating from high school with flying colors, he faced a daunting question: What’s next?
He knew education was his only way out of poverty, yet his family could not afford college. So, he set off for Oman.

“Eventually, I landed my first job in a hotel. From that moment, I never stopped learning. I began setting my sights on the next available position, working hard to be recognized and considered for promotion,” Endozo said.
“Step by step, I rose through the ranks: from waiter to captain, then supervisor, restaurant manager, operations manager, department head, director, and finally general manager.”

He proved to those around him that he deserved every promotion. Competing against professionals of many different nationalities without a college degree or formal background in hospitality, Endozo faced challenges at every turn — yet he prevailed.

Throughout his career, Endozo has worked with some of the world’s most prestigious hotel brands, including InterContinental Hotels, Burj Al Arab, Jumeirah Group, Raffles Hotels, Millennium Hotels, Hilton Worldwide, Citadines, The Ascott, and Fraser Hospitality.
Once he began earning steady money, Endozo started helping his siblings move to Dubai. Eventually, six of them landed good jobs in the city.

“After that, I helped my nephews and nieces, then cousins, then distant relatives, and later even people from our barangay. What started with one person became a chain reaction of helping one another, and today there are more than 120 of us from our family and community working in Dubai,” he said.
Everyone has a story, and Endozo’s shows that poverty and a lack of early resources are not dead ends to reaching your dreams.
“Keep going, keep believing, and never give up,” he said.
Michael Banua holds a degree in chemistry, though he eventually realized his real passion lay elsewhere: storytelling— where his true chemistry is.

Today, Banua is recognized as one of the Top 100 Influencers in the Middle East, with a social media community of more than 230,000 followers as @YourKuyaMico, an award-winning, mentor-driven content platform in the UAE.
It all started during the COVID-19 pandemic with just AED 500 to his name after the company where he worked announced it was shutting down.

“Since I couldn’t travel, I started posting old food photos from my gallery. To my surprise, these received great engagement and positive reactions. Soon, brands noticed my work and began sending complimentary meals in exchange for content,” Banua said.
His very first restaurant review featured a small cafeteria in Karama that served him an AED 12 biryani.

“One day, a restaurant near our office asked how much I charged. Without knowing the industry rates, I confidently said AED 150. That became my first paid collaboration and made me realize content creation could actually become a career,” Banua said.

blocks.caption: Michael Mico Banua

blocks.text: One of his first major collaborations was with a Dubai bottled drinking water company. The campaign brief arrived at 10 pm, and the content had to be delivered by lunchtime the next day.

“Instead of creating a traditional advertisement, I documented my real routine as an OFW — from waking up, preparing for work, commuting on the Metro, spending the day in the office, and ending the day creating food content — while naturally integrating [the bottled water brand] into the story. The campaign stood out because it felt authentic and story-driven rather than promotional,” said Banua.

He landed a follow-up contract with the company, with the campaign appearing on billboards across the UAE — including along Sheikh Zayed Road, the main highway artery — as well as on buses, the Dubai Metro, YouTube ads, cinemas, and other nationwide marketing materials.

That campaign proved to be the turning point in Banua’s career, opening doors to new opportunities — including an invitation from the Dubai Media Office (DMO) to join the #BrandDubai and #DubaiDestinations campaigns promoting the city to the world.

Today, Banua works with leading government entities and brands, including Brand Dubai, Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, Dubai Culture, Sharjah Tourism, the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi, the Abu Dhabi Sports Council, the General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs (GDRFA), the Roads and Transport Authority (RTA), Emirates National Oil Company (ENOC), Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), Miral (Yas Island), Majid Al Futtaim, and Big Ticket.
More importantly, Banua has been paying his success forward by educating and mentoring aspiring content creators inspired by his journey.

“I continue to conduct workshops, with my latest initiative focused on helping Filipino content creators better understand the UAE influencer and content creation landscape,” said Banua, who wears barong tagalog to major events, television appearances, speaking engagements, and UAE campaigns — even those unrelated to the Filipino community — “because representing my culture is something I deeply value.”

“At the heart of everything I do is storytelling, mentorship, and proudly representing the Filipino community while inspiring others to pursue their passions and create opportunities for themselves,” he added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Nigeria: At least 24 dead after boat capsizes
articles.summary: The boat carrying mourners for a funeral overturned in southern Nigeria. It was the latest in a series of deadly boat accidents in the country.

image.caption: The Bayelsa state government has called on boat operators and passengers to follow safety regulations [FILE: August 5, 2026]Image: AFP

blocks.text: A boat capsized in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, the country's emergency agency said on Saturday.
"So far, 24 bodies have been recovered from the scene of the incident, while search and rescue operations are ongoing," said Manzo Ezekiel, a spokesman for the National Emergency Management Agency.
The boat was carrying mourners for a burial ceremony from the town of Ayama to Ukubie in the southern Bayelsa State on Friday when it sank.
Boat reportedly suffered mechanical failure
Authorities have not confirmed how many passengers were on board.
"Those who lost their lives in the tragedy did not deserve to die that way," Nigerian President Bola Tinubu said in a statement on X.
Two children were among the four bodies initially recovered from the water on Friday, when 24 survivors were rescued, according to police.
Police spokesman Musa Mohammed said that preliminary reports suggested that the boat suffered a mechanical problem.
Deadly boat mishaps in Nigeria
Boat accidents are common on Nigeria's busy river networks. Overloading, poor vessel maintenance, and failure to comply with safety norms usually cause them.
In August, at least 51 died after a boat capsized in northwest Nigeria's Sokoto State.
In September 2025, a boat carrying over 100 passengers sank in north-central Niger State, leaving dozens dead.
