articles.title: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
articles.summary: Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

blocks.text: China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.

But in the second draft text of the probably outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”

Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.

But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.
China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.
after newsletter promotion

Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”

China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”

Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”

Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

articles.title: Rejoining EU ‘on the table’ as UK strikes deals on trade and young people
articles.summary:
All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’

The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions…

blocks.text: The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.
The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.
Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were announced after talks this week.
Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU with similar access for Europeans in the UK.
Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.
Miliband said Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next.
He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election.
However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Miliband said in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options”.

Since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the so-called “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement.
Burnham has previously said he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

The prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year plan before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit.
Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”.
“Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he said.” “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.”
On Friday, Burnham said the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”.

He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.
“The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”.
About the further discussions, she said: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”
The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers.
Eagle said: “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and export.
“This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”

articles.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
articles.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.

blocks.text: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media report citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC has contacted the FBI for comment.

This comes after string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks - but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Maria Ressa: Understand AI to defend ourselves from ‘predatory’ tech
articles.summary: 'For those who are saying they cannot act: Don’t fall into learned helplessness. When you are the target, you are powerful,' Rappler CEO Maria Ressa says of the fight against artificial intelligence

blocks.text: FIGHT BACK. Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa delivers a speech during the plenary session of the 2026 Social Good Summit titled 'WE, THE HUMANS: Reclaim Our Future,' at BGC, Taguig City, on November 21, 2026.
Rappler
'For those who are saying they cannot act: Don’t fall into learned helplessness. When you are the target, you are powerful,' Rappler CEO Maria Ressa says of the fight against artificial intelligence

items: Maria Ressa emphasizes the need to understand artificial intelligence to protect against its predatory nature, which she claims is designed to exploit human biology for profit.
She warns that AI is disrupting attention and agency, contributing to a breakdown in societal complexities and accountability, especially in journalism.
Ressa calls for the establishment of facts and truth to protect democracy and highlights the concentration of AI power among a few companies, urging for better oversight and regulation.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Understanding artificial intelligence is essential to defending ourselves from the harms of the “predatory, extractive” technology, Rappler chief executive officer and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa said.
During the 2026 Social Good Summit on Saturday, November 21, Ressa warned that AI was built to “hack our biology” as the end goal of Big Tech is profit.
She explained that AI hacked people’s attention, intimacy, and agency, through machine learning in social media, generative chatbots, and agentic AI.

“What have we lost? Sustained attention… our ability to hold complexity, nuances, to move away from identity politics,” Ressa said in her speech, adding that AI is “shifting the evolution of our species.”
“The technology that we’re getting has essentially been predatory and extractive, like mining. How much data have been given, and where has it gone to?”
That defense should be complemented with building own technologies, according to Ressa. (READ: From Duterte to Big Tech: Maria Ressa’s blueprint on fighting back)
This is after Big Tech is “breaking the social contract” by taking and scraping content from news outfits, pushing the journalism industry to already “reaching market failure.”
In 2025, it was found that bots already drove 53% of internet traffic, according to the latest report of cybersecurity firm Imperva.
“For those who are saying they cannot act: Don’t fall into learned helplessness. When you are the target, you are powerful,” she also said.

Ressa also centered on the continued push to protect democracy by establishing facts and truth, in a bid to “reclaiming our future from the machines we built.” (READ: Maria Ressa on AI overreliance: ‘Don’t outsource the nuances’)

“When you don’t have facts and lies spread faster, you cannot actually solve any problem. Not climate change, not rule of law, not child safety. Because if you don’t have facts, you can’t organize. You can’t hold anyone accountable,” she said.
“The chain of facts is what makes a crowd or a mob into ‘we,’ the people. You break that, and there’s no ‘we’ left to reclaim anything.”
Citing the preliminary report of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, Ressa said AI is changing geopolitical powers.
Ressa is a co-chair of the 40-member panel, which assesses opportunities, risks, and impacts of AI.

“A few hold the future in their hands, five or six companies, and in terms of compute power, the US has 75% of the world’s compute power. China has 15%, and the EU (European Union), which has put in place the safety measures we need, has 5%,” she said.
She also said that the AI deployment is “far outstripping the ability of law, of audit, and of oversight.”

On Monday, November 16, California sued OpenAI, accusing the company of developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had independently carried out cyberattacks. Among this cyberattacks was the July hack of the open-source platform Hugging Face.
In September, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal and gained unauthorized access to files.
“Can we stop impunity in tech?” she asked. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Killer robots' talks at UN end with no legally binding ban
articles.summary: Countries have agreed to extend discussions over controls on lethal autonomous weapons systems for two years.

image.caption: Nearly 100 nations had called for talks on a legally binding agreement [FILE: March 2019]Image: Wolfgang Kumm/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: United Nations talks on regulating lethal autonomous weapons systems ended on Saturday without an agreement on a legally binding ban.
The negotiations did, however, yield an agreement for further discussions to develop new rules by 2028.

Delegates from 128 states that are parties to the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) had been meeting in Geneva since Monday amid rising concerns over the use of the so-called killer robots in global conflicts.
The conference ended early on Saturday in what campaigners deemed a "weakened" outcome, following several hours of overnight parleying.
What happened at the CCW conference?
Nearly 100 nations had called for negotiations on a legally binding agreement on the systems capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Pope Leo XIV and the Red Cross had also supported a ban on killer robots.
However, countries that have the technology, including arms-producing giants like the ​US, Russia ‌and Israel, were among those opposing the mandate.

Ultimately, the 128 countries "agreed to launch the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, which should be conducted over the next two years", the conference's Swiss chair, Julien Thoni, told the media on Saturday.

blocks.caption: Rights groups expressed disappointment at the watered down dealImage: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP

blocks.text: Groups decry a softened mandate on 'killer robots'
But while Thoni hailed a multilateral diplomacy delivering "concrete results" even in "today's deeply divided world," rights groups expressed disappointment at the minimal agreement.

"States adopted a watered-down mandate that fails to chart a clear path towards a legally binding instrument," news agency AFP quoted Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of over 300 organizations, as saying.

"Over 95 states expressed their support for a treaty. In the final hours, a small number of states weakened the mandate introducing uncertainty about the legal status of the final document," it added.
The group had earlier said that autonomous weapons systems were already reaching the battlefield and such systems had been tested or deployed, including in the Ukraine war.

articles.title: Should AI be your personal assistant? Here's what you need to know

image.caption: OpenAI dots and Meta Muse are among the new artificial intelligence agents acting as personal digital assistants. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: Imagine a chatbot that can not only recommend a great restaurant in your area, but can also book a reservation, put it in your calendar and email an invitation to your friends.
In recent months, that scenario has become reality, with some of the world's biggest AI developers launching digital personal assistants they say will make users' lives easier.
The companies behind these new mass market agents say they are remarkably capable, safe and easy to use.
But cybersecurity experts say the more advanced tasks come with more risk that something could go seriously wrong.
What are AI assistants, and how do they work?
Three of most well-known ones on the market — Meta's Muse, OpenAI's dots and Anthropic's Claude Duet — all debuted within weeks of each other and all have similar capabilities.
Muse can be spoken to as if it were a chatbot and instructed to send emails, book travel, make purchases and more on your behalf when connected to third-party apps like Shopify and Ticketmaster.
It can handle multiple tasks at once and continue working through them even while the app is closed.
LISTEN | Tech columnist on her experience using Muse:
The Current21:24What could possibly go wrong with Meta's Muse?

OpenAI says users can instruct dots to do "nearly anything" by messaging or calling them through ChatGPT. They can be connected to other devices and over 4,000 apps, and even have the ability to use your laptop.
Anthropic's Claude Duet has been pitched as more of a proactive agent for work than as an assistant to take on personal errands.

The agent can take on simple administrative tasks, like scheduling meetings, and more complex projects, like creating financial reports or building web apps, according to the company's product announcement.
While Muse is free, dots and Claude Duet each require a subscription. Claude Duet isn't available in Canada yet.
How do AI personal assistants keep your personal info safe?

CBC News reached out to Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic to ask how they protect users' privacy and prevent their personal assistant agents from going beyond the scope of the tasks they're assigned, along with what advice they'd give users to prevent this from happening.

A spokesperson for Meta said Muse runs on its own dedicated computer in the cloud that is designed so users' data is securely stored, referring CBC to a blog post by software engineer Tarek Sheasha outlining the safeguards built into Muse.

They also referred CBC to another blog post that says Muse checks with users before taking on sensitive actions, like sending an email or making a purchase, and shows a complete audit trail of everything the agent has done.

items: People are using AI to 'dumb down' their smart TVs. Is that a good idea?
Google launches AI-based shopping in Canada in race to dominate e-commerce

blocks.text: A spokesperson for OpenAI referred CBC to a blog post outlining its safeguards, which includes encryption for users' content and account security systems that monitor for suspicious use.
OpenAI also monitors dots as they plan and carry out actions "looking for potentially harmful behavior, such as acting outside your instructions or trying to bypass safeguards," the blog post says.

OpenAI also notes that users can give dots custom rules, such as to never send emails, and says certain actions require a user's confirmation each time, such as permanently deleting data and installing or running software from an unrecognized source.
A spokesperson for Anthropic said Claude Duet was built to enable people to stay in control of what it does, and so their information is handled with discretion.

The model never sees users' passwords, browser cookies or sign-in tokens, and Claude Duet is instructed never to share sign-in credentials, credit card and bank account numbers and government ID numbers — even if you ask, the spokesperson said.
What can go wrong?
Some users have reported getting more than they bargained for when putting these high-powered assistants to work.
A Montreal man asked Muse to handle his Facebook Marketplace transactions. But after listing a keyboard for sale, Muse gave out his home address to a stranger without his knowledge.
When the buyer showed up, Muse even told him the seller was there even though he wasn't home.

"Muse doesn't check with me, it doesn't tell me this guy has messaged and then it gives the guy my address, agrees to his price and literally tells him to come right now, that's the crazy part," Matt Robb told CBC News last month.
He used Meta’s AI agent Muse for Marketplace sales. Then it set one up behind his back

Asked how something like this could happen, a spokesperson for Meta pointed CBC to a social media post made by Robb about his ordeal, where he explained he had clicked "allow always" instead of "allow one time" when asking Muse to handle his Marketplace transactions on his behalf going forward.

While these agents can be innovative and exciting tools, they should be used in a limited way and given very specific instructions in order to avoid these kinds of mishaps, said Claudiu Popa, a Toronto-based certified cybersecurity professional with privacy consulting firm Datarisk Canada.
"Unless you tell them very specifically what they can and cannot do you're going to have unpredictable results," he said.
"That's the issue with all AI agents, and this issue is going to continue for the foreseeable future."

items: BMO CEO says don't give AI agents your banking info

blocks.text: David Shipley, CEO and co-founder of Beauceron Security in Fredericton, said he hasn't let these agents get near his computer at all.
"I absolutely do not trust this technology," he said.
Shipley compared trusting them with your personal errands to a monkey's paw wish, referring to the classic horror story that serves as a cautionary tale to be careful what you wish for.
"You might wish for it to do a certain set of actions and it's going to go and do those actions, but perhaps not in the way that you intended it to do that."
Why have Canada's biggest banks blocked AI assistants?
With a client's authorization, AI agents can also connect to bank accounts and credit cards to monitor balances and transaction histories and give tips on budgeting.

But concerns over AI agents accessing sensitive information have also prompted Royal Bank, TD Bank, CIBC and Bank of Montreal to block them from directly accessing their clients' online bank accounts and other information.
The CEOs of RBC and BMO recently warned that third-party AI agents are not to be trusted with personal banking information.
Why banks are banning AI agents
Those warnings should give people pause about using these agents entirely, given that banks "have been among the more fervent adopters of digital technology over the last 30 years," Shipley said.

But Popa said he thinks these AI personal assistants can be used in a limited way without compromising your personal information, such as for tasks like research or writing emails — not sending them — for you.

"You can't necessarily trust an outside AI agent with your private information. So sharing calendars, emails, all sorts of personal information and personal files, that is for me, it's not a line that I would let it cross."

articles.title: Beyond the classroom, UPLB skaters carve out space in town with no skatepark
articles.summary: While skateboarding has gained national recognition through athletes like Olympian Margielyn Didal, access to dedicated skating spaces remains a concern for local communities

blocks.text: Tambay lang ‘yan (They’re just loitering). Banchi Jimena wants people to stop seeing skaters this way.

Banchi, 22, is a University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) student and skate filmmaker. Los Baños has no dedicated outdoor skatepark, according to local skaters. So he and his friends skate wherever they can on campus.

One of their favorite spots is the rooftop of a parking garage near Christian School International. Others are hidden behind the Institute of Biological Sciences (IBS) building and the buildings around the College of Engineering and Agro-Industrial Technology (CEAT) in UPLB. Campus security has caught them several times.
“Kilalang-kilala na kami (They know us very well by now),” he said.

Jules, a UPLB student and beginner skater, ran into problems early. They had hoped to skate between classes as an eco-friendly way to get around. The roads turned out to be less suitable than they expected.
Finding people to skate with is just as hard. Banchi has seen a livelier scene in town and wants to bring it back. Jules usually skates alone and is still looking for others to learn from.
Skateboarding has gained national recognition through athletes like Olympian Margielyn Didal. Access to dedicated skating spaces, however, remains a concern for local communities.
In Los Baños, skaters make do with spaces meant for other purposes. Finding other skaters is its own problem.
“Patay talaga ‘yung scene dito sa LB kaya sa Manila ako lagi (The scene here in LB is really dead, so I’m always in Manila),” Banchi said.
Before Banchi and Jules can skate, they first have to find somewhere to roll.
Banchi sees the search for spots as part of the fun. He compares skating to traveling, with a good street spot as the destination.
During his year off from school, his work took him to many places. He found new spots and made new friends along the way.
“Nakakapag-travel ka, na-enjoy mo pa ‘yung ginagawa mo (You get to travel, and you enjoy what you’re doing too),” he said.
Back in Los Baños, there are fewer options. Banchi said he has already explored most of the spots on campus.
Jules also found fewer places to skate than they expected. They usually skate in a parking lot within walking distance of where they stay. They also stick to places where skating is not prohibited.

Security is another concern. Banchi said guards treat skaters differently. Some understand skaters even if they don’t skate themselves. Others are only doing their job. In Los Baños, he said, guards have been less understanding.
Luckily, Jules has not been asked to leave a spot so far.
“Mahirap talaga. Pero kung skater ka, kumbaga, gagawa ka talaga ng paraan (It’s really hard. But if you’re a skater, you’ll really find a way),” Banchi said.
Still, a spot is only half of it. The other half is having people to skate with.

blocks.caption: COMMUNITY. Banchi (left) says it’s important to have a crew who believes in you. Photos from Banchi Jimena’s Instagram page

blocks.text: Banchi still remembers what the Los Baños scene used to be like.
“Dati, buhay na buhay (It used to be so alive),” he said.
Some of the skaters who anchored it can still be seen in front of CSI. Banchi looks up to them like older brothers. Most of them no longer skate.
So when he spotted someone skateboarding in town while out on a walk not long ago, he was glad.
“Nakakagulat na may nagi-skate pa pala dito (It’s surprising that people still skate here),” he said.
A few skaters still gather in the bayan. Jules has noticed that they usually come out only on weekends or on random days. When they do, they seem busy, which makes them hard to approach.
Jules ends up skating alone most of the time, learning without anyone around to guide them.
“My biggest challenge is finding a community and learning properly,” they said.
Banchi was not always sure he belonged either. When he started skating, he was the weakest in his group. He had always loved cameras, so he started filming his friends instead.
“Para lang mabilang ako doon sa group (Just so I could be counted in that group),” he said.

That was how his passion for filmmaking began. His full-length skate film, What The Sigma, was later named Skate Film of the Year 2025 at the first Silog Skate Awards, according to Silog Skate Magazine.
Today, he believes what keeps skaters going is having a crew that believes you can do it. It is also why he wants to bring the scene back.
“Gusto ko talaga buhayin ‘yung scene dito (I really want to bring the scene here back to life),” he said.
Their stories show two sides of the same gap. Banchi remembers a scene worth saving. Jules is still waiting to find one.
Banchi wants to change how people see skaters.
“Ayoko lang talagang ma-discriminate ‘yung mga skater (I just really don’t want skaters to be discriminated against),” he said.
Jules also sees skaters as a “very stigmatized community, very misunderstood.”

Within the community itself, there is debate over what skating should be. According to Banchi, some older skaters want younger ones to become competition skaters, partly so the sport looks more proper and gets judged less.

He disagrees. Not every Filipino can afford a skateboard, he said, and he believes there are too few skateparks in the country. Pushing kids to become athletes also goes against what skating meant to those same older skaters when they were young, he added.
Banchi sees skating as closer to art than sport. It is a lifestyle, something done freely, the way someone might draw.
“Wala kasi dapat pressure pag nags-skate (There shouldn’t be any pressure when you skate),” he said.
Banchi has thought about what a skatepark could do for Los Baños. Skaters from other places would start coming to town, he said, and the local skater population would grow.
He believes a park would also give parents, including professors, a safer place than the streets to bring kids who want to skate.

He points to the skatepark in Quezon City, which he said was built beside a pickleball court. Many passersby, he said, grew curious about why it was there. A park in Los Baños could spark the same curiosity, he added, and show young people there is more to sports than basketball.
“Hindi lang basketball ang buhay (Life isn’t just about basketball),” he said.

Jules sees a park as a way to change minds. Skateboarding is still a niche sport in the Philippines, they said. Placing a park in a busy area could clear up some of the stigma and misunderstanding around it.
Until then, Banchi and his friends keep searching for spots around campus, while Jules practices wherever he can.
Some people may still call them tambay. They keep skating anyway.
Banchi’s advice to fellow students is to open their minds and unlock skills they never got to try as kids.
“Enjoy mo lang ‘yung buhay mo (Just enjoy your life),” he said. – Rappler.com
Arabella Grace Sta. Ana is a Rappler intern studying BA Philosophy at UP Los Baños.

articles.title: A Canadian study pinned a baby's death on codeine passed through breast milk. 20 years on, it's been retracted
articles.summary: A highly influential yet controversial Canadian study that linked a baby's death to codeine passed through breastmilk — and informed global guidance on breastfeeding and pain management over the last…

image.caption: The Lancet medical journal has retracted Gideon Koren's controversial 2006 study that pinned a baby’s death on codeine passed through breast milk. (CBC/Freepik)

blocks.text: Health·New

A highly influential yet controversial Canadian study that linked a baby's death to codeine passed through breastmilk — and informed global guidance on breastfeeding and pain management over the last two decades — has been pulled from a leading medical journal, which said omissions in the research amounted to "falsification."
Omissions amounting to 'falsification' identified in influential 2006 study, The Lancet journal medical says

A highly influential yet controversial Canadian study that linked a baby's death to codeine passed through breast milk — and informed global guidance on breastfeeding and pain management over the last two decades — has been pulled from a leading medical journal, which said omissions in the research amounted to "falsification."

In the latest issue of The Lancet, set for release Nov. 21, the journal announced it has retracted the 2006 paper by Gideon Koren, the once esteemed founder of the Motherisk drug testing lab at the Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) in Toronto.

The saga involving Koren's long-questioned study included years of Canadian media coverage, a sweeping New Yorker investigation last January, and a decision by The Lancet to add an "expression of concern" to the case report in February following new allegations of falsified toxicological data, authorship issues and ethical concerns.
The case focused on the deadly poisoning of an Ontario infant in 2005.

The study purported that the boy's mother was prescribed the painkiller Tylenol 3, which contains both acetaminophen and codeine — a mild opioid that gets partially metabolized into morphine inside the body — causing a deadly amount of morphine to pass to the boy through her breast milk.

items: Why a 20-year-old study claiming a baby died from opioid poisoning through breast milk is still under fire

blocks.text: Koren long insisted the case showed maternally ingested codeine can be fatal for breastfeeding infants, despite mounting questions about that likelihood from other pediatricians and toxicologists.

"This paper is the cornerstone of an entire field of pediatric pharmacology and toxicology that, honestly, should not exist," said Toronto-based internist and pharmacologist Dr. David Juurlink, a longtime critic of what he called a "botched" study on a coroner's investigation.

"This isn't just about one mischaracterized infant death. The narrative that babies can die through opioids passed through breast milk has greatly influenced postpartum pain care. It has caused women taking opioids to forgo breastfeeding, thereby depriving infants of the benefits of breastfeeding, which are numerous."
Tainted Tests: Broken Families
'Omitted findings' in case report

The Lancet's retraction notice said the journal had received the "outcome and conclusion" of a formal investigation from SickKids' research integrity office after referring its allegations to the Toronto hospital.
"The authorship issues and ethical concerns could not be fairly investigated as a meaningful participation of Gideon Koren was unlikely to be possible," reads the notice.

"On the allegation of omission of material toxicological data, including the infant's blood codeine and acetaminophen concentrations and the qualitative identification of codeine in the infant's stomach contents, the report concluded that this omission constitutes falsification. The omitted findings left readers without the information necessary to assess the publication's conclusion."
It's just the latest blow against Koren, who relinquished his medical licence in Ontario after a scandal-filled career that included the closure of the Motherisk lab in 2019.

The facility gained worldwide attention for using hair strands to test for drug and alcohol use in mothers — methods deemed "inadequate and unreliable" by an independent provincial review in 2015, but not before they were used in thousands of child protection cases and broke apart families across the country.

items: How the flawed Motherisk hair test helped fracture families across Canada
Hair test evidence tossed out of Colorado court 2 decades before questions raised in Canada

blocks.text: CBC News has contacted Koren for comment.
In a statement to CBC News following The Lancet's retraction notice, a spokesperson for SickKids said the facility "takes all matters of research integrity seriously."

The hospital's formal inquiry concluded material toxicological data had been omitted from the published report and determined that this "constituted falsification under SickKids' Responsible Conduct of Research Policy." The hospital declined to provide further details on the findings, due to the "confidential nature of research integrity inquiries."

items: Motherisk scandal highlights risk of deferring to experts without questioning credentials

blocks.text: The Lancet's retraction notice has been "a long time coming," Juurlink said.

"It's surprising that it took such a long time for this to happen. Not just that it took a long time, but that it took investigative journalism to cast a light on the institutional failures that kept this paper alive for 20 years."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lauren Pelley is a senior health and medical reporter for CBC News. She's a two-time RNAO Media Award winner for in-depth health reporting in 2020 and 2022, a silver medallist for best editorial newsletter at the 2024 Digital Publishing Awards, and a 2024 Covering Climate Now award winner in the health category. Contact her at: lauren.pelley@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Israeli settler violence at unprecedented levels during Palestinian olive harvest
articles.summary: There have been more settler attacks against Palestinians and their property during this year’s olive harvest than in 20 years of record-keeping by the United Nations.

image.caption: Israeli settlers, clad mainly in black, stand near a fire amid clashes during the olive harvest in Abu Falah, near Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)

blocks.text: "It’s so random and doesn’t have any rules. You don’t know where it could come from, or in which intensity. Which weapon, how many?"
Wala Zoran is talking about attacks by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank during the annual olive harvest.

We met her on Oct. 11 while she was standing with a group of fellow Palestinians, warily watching some settlers standing alongside Israeli soldiers on the other side of an olive grove in the village of Abu Mash’al. One settler had a rifle slung across his back.
Zoran and her family, including her elderly grandparents, were attacked by settlers in the grove the day before while trying to harvest their olives.

"They started throwing big stones at us and we realized that we can’t take the olives — we can’t take anything, actually," she said. "We started running, but they were so close. Everybody was hit with the stones, like my father, my sister. I was. My cousin was shot in the leg, actually, and had to spend the night in hospital."
Wala Zoran and her family were attacked by settlers on Oct. 10, while trying to harvest their olives in the West Bank village of Abu Mash’al. (CBC)
This despite their efforts to avoid a confrontation.
There have been more settler attacks against Palestinians and their property during this year’s olive harvest than in 20 years of record-keeping by the United Nations.

Like many Palestinians, Zoran’s family has changed how they harvest in a bid to stay safe. They try to gather their olives in quick bursts, not waiting until the big tarpaulins they put on the ground to catch the olives are full before ferrying them back home.
They also wait to begin picking until other families from the village are able to join.
But safety in numbers isn’t working.

Israeli soldiers and settlers are seen side by side in Abu Mash’al in the Occupied West Bank. According to the United Nations, Israeli settler attacks, often with Israeli military protection, numbered close to 400 for October alone. (CBC)
'People depend on olive oil here'
Zoran lives in France but returns home to help her family with the annual harvest. She’s worried her parents will have to make another attempt this year to finish the harvest.
"People depend on olive oil here," she said. "We can’t just say, 'OK, I don’t feel like doing it this year.'"
The olive industry contributes up to 15 per cent of agricultural GDP in the Palestinian economy.

A family harvests olives in the Palestinian town of Beit Surik, on the western edge of the occupied West Bank. Some groves lie behind the separation barrier built by Israel in the early 2000s, which snakes onto Palestinian land in some parts, cutting farmers off from their trees. (CBC)
On the other side of the family's olive grove, the IDF soldiers eventually left after lobbing tear gas into the trees where a few Palestinians had remained.
The settlers then gathered up the olives left behind and drove off with them in the direction of what’s known as an outpost.

All Israeli settlements in the occupied territories, including East Jerusalem, are illegal under international law. Israel continues to expand them while also tolerating — and often facilitating — a growing number of outposts, small camps from which Jewish extremists try to push Palestinians from their land. Even Israel considers them illegal, at least on paper.
More than 180 outposts have been created since 2023, according to the Israeli settlement watch group Peace Now, many of them close to Palestinian population centres.

Political analyst and researcher Ibrahim Rabaya’a says it’s one reason violence is surging during this year’s harvest. He describes the speed with which the outposts are spreading as a "strategic escalation" by settlers emboldened by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanhayu and his far-right government.

"We are talking about … a very organized process, very organized players," said Rabaya’a during an interview at his home in Ramallah. "[The settlers] are well-trained. They are working in general as an army, militias."
'Every single day we have attacks'

It's especially striking how emboldened the settlers are compared to even a year ago — whether in groups of two or three harassing Palestinian herders and their livestock or forming battle lines in large numbers, masked and terrifying.
CBC News witnessed the latter while visiting Abu Falah, one of a cluster of villages in the central West Bank, on Oct. 13.
Palestinian farmers risk their lives to pick their olives
We arrived just a few hours after settlers had descended from a hilltop outpost above the town and taken axes to dozens of olive trees.
The residents had blocked the road leading from the base of the hill into the town with heavy stones to stop the settlers from going any further by vehicle.

When the Palestinians led our news crew to see the damaged trees on foot, the settlers spotted us and started back down the hill, some on foot, running at full speed with sticks and slingshots. Others were driven down in the backs of white pickup trucks. They were masked and dressed in black.

When the call went out to Abu Falah’s residents to defend their groves, they picked up rocks of their own on the way, moving through the olive trees to the outer perimeter, later firing firecrackers at the settlers as they advanced.
"Every single day we have attacks and every single day we’re out in the field defending people," said Diyaa Murra, a university student volunteering with the Palestinian Red Crescent.

Palestinian emergency services are under increased pressure during the harvest, with the Israeli NGO Yesh Din charting more than 25 settler incidents a day during the harvest, from vandalism to physical assault.
Ambulances try to position themselves in areas where repeat attacks take place to avoid being delayed by Israeli military checkpoints or imposed closures.

"I think the only way to defend ourselves from the settlers is to engage with everybody in defending the village," said Murra, who was born in Abu Falah. "So I decided to work with the Red Crescent to be part of the defence system. That’s the only way."
The melee continued in Abu Falah until the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) arrived, firing tear gas canisters in the direction of the Palestinians retreating from the bottom of the hill.
Israeli settlers attack and beat Palestinians, U.S. journalist in West Bank

A few days later, the settlers attacked Abu Falah again, making international headlines after a U.S. photojournalist for the Washington Post named Heidi Levine was severely beaten by settlers who surrounded her.
Violence affects livelihood
Before we left Abu Falah on the day we visited, we counted at least 40 settlers involved in the attack clearly visible and back up on top of the hill.
Yet we witnessed only one arrest: a Palestinian man handcuffed and blindfolded as Israeli soldiers led him toward a military vehicle.
Later, we learned the father of five had been held for three days and fined for throwing stones.
The Palestinians say they have little else with which to defend themselves.

"[Palestinians know] most of the settlers are protected by the army," said Mohammad Ahmad, a Palestinian American waiting for the olives he managed to collect to be processed at a mill in Silwad, a town about 10 kilometres from Abu Falah.
"Even the young settlers [… ] under the age of 18 and 17 years old, they have weapons, you know."
Olives picked in the West Bank are processed at a mill in Silwad, a town about 10 kilometres from Abu Falah. (CBC)
Ahmad says this season’s violence is impacting livelihoods and yields, including his own.
"I have never experienced or felt the way we’re feeling right now, because of the settlers and because of what’s going on," he said. "And we’re not allowed to reach most of our lands."
Tensions with IDF
Many Palestinians are required to co-ordinate access to their own olive trees with the IDF, depending on where they’re located.

On Tuesday, the IDF issued a statement on social media saying that 90 per cent of what it called "co-ordinated harvests" had been completed. It also denied claims that security forces were deliberately preventing the olive harvest.
The Palestinian Farmers Union responded, saying that as of late October, 55 per cent of the overall olive crop "remained inaccessible or unharvested."
Israeli forces arrived early in the morning of October 21st, keeping the Palestinian villagers of Deir Jarir from reaching their olive groves. (CBC)
Israeli security forces can often declare areas of confrontation between Palestinians and settlers closed military zones.
That’s what happened when our crew arrived in Deir Jarir, another town in the central West Bank, on Oct. 21.
After settlers ambushed an initial attempt to harvest olives, the Palestinians invited Israeli and international activists to accompany them on a second try, hoping they might offer protection.
But when they arrived at the muster point carrying ladders and olive rakes, the villagers found an armoured vehicle and a handful of IDF soldiers blocking the road.
"They are telling us that our farms are closed military zones and we cannot leave, and we’re stuck here," 72-year-old Abu Asif told CBC News.
The IDF has said its security forces operate to "prevent friction and violence, enabling residents to harvest safely."
In some instances, Israeli soldiers themselves have uprooted entire olive groves, saying they could be used by Palestinians to hide in and as a launching point for attacks.
Palestinians say it’s simply one more way Israel is trying to remove them from their land.
"Our life under occupation has always been difficult," said Abu Asif. "But this time, this season, it’s the most difficult and the hardest."
'The Palestinians are defenceless'
Prime Minister Netanyahu has dismissed the settler attacks as the work of a "small minority."
But Israeli lawyer and peace activist Daniel Seideman says that what’s happening in the West Bank couldn’t be done without Netanyahu's "knowledge, consent and blessing."

"The Palestinians are defenceless," he said in an interview at his office in Jerusalem. "The military is either in bed with the settlers, doing the settlers' bidding or turning a blind eye and saying, 'This isn’t our responsibility.'"
"It’s clear that the settlers see this as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to ethnically cleanse the West Bank," Seideman said, adding that he didn’t use the term lightly.

Seideman spoke to CBC News ahead of last month’s Israeli election, which many believed would see Netanyahu’s tenure come to an end. At the time of publication, it's still unclear who will ultimately form a government.
Analyst Ibrahim Rabaya’a says while a change in government could rein in some of the settler violence, few Palestinians believe it would slow the de facto annexation of the West Bank.
"It is also a strategy for other political players in Israel, but they try to do so without bringing anger from international society," he said. "What we can [call] silent annexation."
Political analyst Ibrahim Rabaya’a says the proliferation of settler outposts in the West Bank is one reason violence is surging during this year’s olive harvest. (CBC)
None of the other main Jewish political parties are on the record supporting a Palestinian state, although Yair Golan’s Democrats have indicated they would potentially support it in the future.
The olive harvest is a favourite target for Israeli hard-liners, precisely because it is such a potent cultural symbol of Palestinians' connection to the land.
Israeli flags everywhere
Rabaya’a says that in addition to the daily hardships of living under occupation, the settlers have been trying to increase psychological pressure on Palestinians.
Over the past several months, Israeli flags have started appearing along the main road from Ramallah up to the northern cities of Nablus and Jenin.
Settlers are using Israeli flags as new intimidation tactic in the West Bank
And along that road in the town of Luban al Sharqiya, settlers arrived one night in October to completely swamp a Palestinian roadside café with Israeli flags.
The owner, Muayad Hussein, who lives with his family in a house just behind the café, says that when he heard them, he was too afraid to come out.

He showed CBC News the images captured by his security camera: dozens of young Jewish extremists pounding the flags into the ground. An Israeli police car can be seen parked on the other side of the road. Someone hands out drinks as they work.
Hussein told us one of the settlers from a nearby outpost warned him that if he took the flags down, they would come back.
He’s afraid they will. So the flags remain.
Muayad Hussein, who owns a roadside café in the town of Luban al Sharqiya, looks at the Israeli flags that were hammered into the ground outside his shop by a group of settlers. (CBC)

articles.title: Allies are buying Canadian underwater surveillance drones. Canada is 'not there yet'
articles.summary: Canada has a three-ocean coastline — 243,000 kilometres — and only 20 underwater drones to help defend it. The navy's commander confirms there isn't a solution ready a year after an internal document…

image.caption: B.C.-based Cellula Robotics said its long-range underwater drone called Guardian is about the size of a 12-metre shipping container. The company's CEO Neil Manning says it's capable of 5,000-kilometre missions or staying offshore for up to 45 days. Five NATO allies have bought it, he said. (Cellula

blocks.text: Canada has a three-ocean, 243,000-kilometre coastline and about 20 underwater drones to help defend it.
Defence officials talked last year about the need for a short-term fix to assert Canada's sovereignty, according to an internal document obtained by CBC News.
But the Royal Canadian Navy's commander, Vice-Admiral Dan Charlebois, confirms there isn't an interim solution ready.
"We're still working very closely with industry to get there. We're just not there yet," said Charlebois in an interview with CBC News.

The navy wanted to see if Canadian underwater drones could help address surveillance gaps along the "sparsely" monitored coast until its first uncrewed underwater surveillance system is ready, the paper obtained through an access-to-information request said.

The navy's current small fleet of American underwater drones is equipped with tech built by Canadian company Kraken Robotics. But the navy uses those drones for mine hunting and testing, not surveillance.
Kraken and B.C.-based Cellula Robotics are viewed as world leaders in underwater drone technology and already selling their systems to allies around the globe for surveillance. But not yet to Canada.
Canada makes underwater drones, so why isn’t it using them?
Other countries are racing to monitor and protect critical underwater cables from potential acts of sabotage by adversaries.

A massive network of these communication cables runs along ocean floors, carrying more than 95 per cent of the world's internet traffic and trillions in financial transactions. Damage could cripple societies.
Hundreds of submarine cables run along ocean floors around the world. These fiber-optic cables have allegedly been targeted by adversaries. (Kevin Kirk/CBC)
University of Calgary defence expert Rob Huebert said Canada has "very significant vulnerabilities" because it can't fully detect when adversaries are entering Canadian waters.
Canada has long relied, Huebert said, on co-operation with the U.S. Navy as a safety net and allowed its fleets, submarines and satellites to age and deteriorate.

"The backstop that I think Canadian governments have always counted on was of course, if we were slow, if we were late on any of these surveillance capabilities off our coastline, well the Americans would take care of it," Huebert said.
He called that a "policy of hope."
The navy is undergoing its biggest peacetime fleet renewal since the Second World War. But some replacements aren't coming until the 2030s and 2040s.

items: What NATO patrols are watching in the Baltic Sea after undersea cables were severed

blocks.text: Ottawa's in the initial procurement phase for a $250-million to $499-million underwater surveillance system that uses drones and sensors to detect, monitor and gather intelligence about threats. The system is expected to be used in Canadian waters, including the Arctic, and during deployments abroad.

"We expect to take delivery of some large autonomous vehicles in the early 2030s," Charlebois said. "That is just around the corner when you're talking about delivering a very advanced large-scale system."
The Royal Canadian Navy's commander, Vice-Admiral Dan Charlebois, says the navy is testing out drone technology. (Mathieu Theriault/CBC)
The government wants the system fully delivered by 2043. But it isn't clear yet if foreign companies will be able to bid on the project.
When asked about the obstacles to finding an interim solution, Charlebois said the procurement system "can be challenging," but he's seen an appetite from Ottawa to cut down on red tape.
"The products that the navy needs exist here in Canada," he said. "We just have to enable ourselves to actually procure them and procure them at pace."
Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to speed up procurement through the Defence Investment Agency. He's also vowed to massively scale up drone production.
Canada has 2,000 drones or so in its inventory, Carney said earlier this fall. But he said the country will need millions in the years to come.
'Not there yet': Why Canada's navy lags in underwater drone tech

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the government is creating a roster of preapproved companies for sole-source contracting. The navy says this will open up "new opportunities" to work with the industry on underwater drones.
Allies using tech to monitor underwater cables

Off the coast of Halifax, Dave Shea, the executive vice-president of strategy and growth at Kraken Robotics, said one of the biggest challenges his company has faced in Canada is the pace of procurement. But he is excited the government wants to speed it up.
His company outfitted the navy's small fleet of drones with synthetic aperture sonar systems.

Those sonar systems, Shea said, scan the sea floor for objects of interest and take high-resolution images. Kraken's technology can also listen for any submarines or boats operating in the area, he said.

The Kraken Robotics underwater drone Katfish is designed to be towed by a boat. It carries a synthetic aperture sonar system that can take high-resolution images of the seabed. The Royal Danish Navy, the Polish Navy and Royal Australian Navy use this technology. (David Laughlin/CBC)
In recent years, Shea said allies have pivoted to use their technology to monitor if underwater cables or pipelines have been tampered with.
Canada could too, he said, but would need a much bigger fleet and longer-range drones because the coastline is so vast.

"There's a lot of technologies that are being built and delivered by companies like Kraken … that could be deployed directly here in Canada to help understand what's actually happening, who's in our waterways, who's in our sovereign waters and what are the risks to be able to protect Canadian capabilities," Shea said.
Orders headed to Europe, U.S., Asia
Cellula Robotics CEO Neil Manning says his company has sold its long-range drone to five NATO allies, but not Canada.
Systems are on order and will be heading to Europe, the U.S. and Asia, he said.
Cellula Robotics says its Guardian drones can carry out long-endurance missions. (Submitted by Cellula Robotics)
Cellula uses hydrogen fuel cell technology, Manning said, that's been adapted from NASA's space launches to work in the water.
The company's long-range drones can travel up to 5,000 kilometres or stay out at sea for up to 45 days, he said.
"I'm highly confident that we will see domestic spend as well," Manning said. "But at the moment we're still in that cycle of building trust with with our local governments."
'We need to get further ahead'
Charlebois is aware critical infrastructure is being challenged elsewhere in the world and said he's trying to get ahead of the problem.
"This is why we're working more closely with Canadian industry than I've seen in my 34 years in the navy because we know we need to get further ahead in this space than we are," he said.
The navy's fleet diving unit put an underwater drone in the water to practice looking for mines in 2021 off the coast of Halifax. (Master Cpl. Anthony Laviolette/Canadian Armed Forces)
Canada contributes to underwater surveillance capabilities with the U.S., Charlebois said, that deliver a "really high level" of awareness, but he wants to do more and is prioritizing sensors.
Asked why Canada is lagging behind protecting underwater infrastructure, Defence Minister David McGuinty said the government is working on it.

"I say that we're rebuilding all of our capacity underwater, on land, in the air and connected to satellites," McGuinty said. "We're building a combined layered approach to being able to understand and identify what might be coming at Canada."
The navy said it has a layered network of capabilities to protect this infrastructure, but noted the government, owners and allies are also responsible.

articles.title: Elon Musk looks to break up with MAGA. To what end?
articles.summary: Elon Musk has certainly seemed to embrace the Make America Great Again movement. Why does that matter? Because the Tesla and Space X CEO now appears to be distancing himself.

image.caption: Elon Musk listens as Donald Trump speaks at a campaign event on Oct. 5, 2024, in Butler, Pa. Since spending a record amount of money on losing candidates during this month's midterms, the world's richest man has said he is 'not MAGA.' (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Elon Musk has certainly seemed to embrace the Make America Great Again movement. Why does that matter? Because the Tesla and Space X CEO now appears to be distancing himself.
'I'm not MAGA', Musk said this week, 2 years after declaring himself 'dark MAGA'

From his first time donning a black MAGA hat and declaring himself "dark MAGA" at an October 2024 rally for Donald Trump to his multimillon-dollar splurge on Republican candidates ahead of this month's midterms, Elon Musk has certainly seemed to embrace the Make America Great Again movement.
Why does that matter? Because the Tesla and Space X CEO now appears to be distancing himself from his MAGA bonafides, saying that he never really considered himself a MAGA adherent.
"I'm not MAGA," Musk declared earlier this week, in an interview with The New York Times.

"I'm not sure what MAGA means," he said during the newspaper's DealBook Summit. "If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties."
That may come as a surprise considering Musk made at least five appearances between 2024 and 2025 in which he associated himself with the movement, according to Mediaite, a news website.

items: Elon Musk gets little bang for his buck in U.S. midterms, with possible Democratic investigations to come

blocks.text: But Musk's MAGA split appears to come at a time when association to the brand could prove to be a business and legal liability for the world's richest man.
"It's so transparently convenient," said Matthew Dallek, a professor of political management and historian at the D.C.-based George Washington University, who has researched the MAGA movement.
Musk's comments follow the Republicans' disastrous showing in the U.S. midterms and the so-called Democratic blue wave that saw the party take control of the House and the Senate.
Along with MAGA-boosting appearances, Musk also spent more than $400 million U.S. on Trump-aligned Republican candidates in the midterms — the most money of any individual campaign donor.
Can Musk disassociate from MAGA?
"Now that [MAGA]'s on the losing side, all of a sudden, he's not MAGA," said Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University.
"I mean, come on. This is just laughable. This is the guy who glossed himself 'dark MAGA' and had black MAGA stuff put together ... when Trump took over. He was completely in with it."
Prof. Matthew Dallek says Elon Musk, seen speaking before Donald Trump at a campaign rally on Oct. 27, 2024, made his 'MAGA bed' and now must lie in it. (Evan Vuccu/The Associated Press)
Dallek said Musk has spent years making his "MAGA bed."
"Now he's got to lie in it, even when it's politically uncomfortable."

Musk, who also urged his followers on X to vote Republican, now says he feels "pretty foolish" for spending so much money on the midterms. He also said in his NYT interview that ideologically he is "quite moderate" and doesn't have any "extreme political views."
But Dallek said if he's really such a moderate and not part of the MAGA ranks, there were non-MAGA Republicans he could have backed during the elections.
Instead, Musk spent around $200 million US backing Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who Dallek called, "arguably the most MAGA of all the midterm candidates."

items: Elon Musk calls documentary about him a 'hit piece' after buzzy debut
Satellite limitations imposed by Musk's SpaceX pose danger for Ukraine, Zelenskyy says

blocks.text: Musk has based himself and several of his companies in Texas, including Tesla, SpaceX ‌and a planned chipmaking venture between the two. But the state is almost all blue following the U.S. midterms.
"The government is no longer in the hands of his allies," Dallek said. "He is in a very vulnerable position. Businesses are very vulnerable."

Dallek also questioned just how "moderate" Musk is, as he's has turned X into a platform for extremist views. As well, a February 2025 NBC News report said Musk had been encouraging right-wing political movements, policies and administrations in at least 18 countries as part of a global push to slash immigration and curtail regulation of business.
"It's just transparently false when he says, 'I'm a moderate,'" Dallek said.
What's driving Musk's MAGA retreat?
One reason: The MAGA brand is at its lowest net favourability ever, said CNN’s chief data analyst Harry Enten.
"It is a brand that is failing amongst the American public," he said.
But perhaps more importantly, Musk may be trying to engender better relations with Democrats as he faces government probes and red tape.
Alex Gibney warns of Elon Musk's 'unchecked power' in new documentary
Democrats have indicated they may want to investigate the months Musk spent in 2025 spearheading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).
DOGE team activities led to widespread dismantling of foreign aid programs, as well as allegations that team members breached privacy laws by illegally accessing the sensitive data of Americans.
Musk may also face slower approvals for the billions of dollars Space X plans to invest in data centre campuses in Texas and Arizona.

"They're going to be turning their eyes toward him and his space facilities, and the environmental issues that they're causing and tax issues," Belt said. "Things that could really make life difficult for him. He doesn't want to poke the bear."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Mark Gollom is a Toronto-based reporter with CBC News. He covers Canadian and U.S. politics and current affairs.
With files from The Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Canada's first climate lawsuit to go to trial has wrapped up hearings. Many more are underway
articles.summary: What level of responsibility does the federal government bear for the climate disasters Canadians are suffering? That's the question at the heart of a landmark lawsuit that wrapped up witness…

image.caption: A climate rally in Vancouver in September 2023. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Science

What level of responsibility does the federal government bear for the climate disasters Canadians are suffering? That's the question at the heart of a landmark lawsuit that wrapped up witness testimony in Federal Court in Vancouver on Friday, and whose outcome could have a big influence on how a growing number of other climate lawsuits in Canada pan out.
Youth lawsuit in Federal Court paves way for other cases questioning governments' duty to ensure safe climate
What level of responsibility does the federal government bear for the climate disasters Canadians are suffering?

That's the question at the heart of a landmark lawsuit that wrapped up witness testimony in Federal Court in Vancouver on Friday, and whose outcome could have a big influence on how a growing number of other climate lawsuits in Canada pan out.

La Rose et al. v Canada, brought by 15 youth applicants in 2019 who say the federal government's inadequate actions to reduce carbon emissions is violating their constitutional rights, was heard over the past five weeks — the first full trial for a climate lawsuit in Canada.
A dozen expert witnesses testified, along with the young people themselves.

items: Historic lawsuit challenging government over climate inaction begins trial hearings

blocks.text: Andrea Rodgers, deputy director at Our Children's Trust, a legal non-profit that's supporting the case, said it's been "an incredible journey" for the plaintiffs and she hopes the case will inspire "a body of law that will continue to evolve."

"I think if there's one thing many people can agree on, it's that the interests of our children should be prioritized and protected. And this case gives the courts in Canada the opportunity to do that for Canadian youth," Rodgers said Friday.
But even as the historic hearings took place, more cases of climate-related litigation appeared.

On Nov. 18, a lawsuit was filed against the province of Quebec for delaying an emissions target. A lawsuit to force Canada's largest pension fund to better manage climate risk had an important hearing in November.

Two other cases — a youth lawsuit seeking a more stringent climate plan in Ontario and a Federal Court case arguing the federal government is not following its own climate law — are also chugging along.
Can you sue Canada for not doing enough about climate change?
Lawsuits building off each other

Fraser Thomson, a lawyer at environmental law charity Ecojustice, said as the various cases have gone through the court system, they've "built off each other" by winning legal arguments to pave the way for following cases.

"As more and more courts look at the indisputable evidence that shows that climate change poses an existential threat, courts are increasingly choosing to entertain these arguments and in some cases to weigh in favour of them on certain legal issues," Thomson said.
Thomson is not involved in La Rose, but he is a lawyer for the plaintiffs in a newly filed federal lawsuit, Maltais et al. v Canada, as well as a long running Ontario case, Mathur et al. v Ontario.

Mathur was filed in 2019 after Ontario Premier Doug Ford's government weakened the province's emissions targets. The plaintiffs argued that exposed them to climate harms and violated their constitutional rights to life, liberty and security, as well as equality. The case was initially dismissed by the first level of court, but then sent back for a full hearing by the appeal court.

Right before Mathur was to receive a hearing in 2025 , the Ford government repealed the law requiring it to set an emissions target at all, and the case was put on hold. Thomson said he hopes to be back in front of a judge in early 2027 to get some clarity on the path forward.
A rally outside the International Court of Justice in 2025 ahead of an advisory opinion on what legal obligations nations have to address climate change. (Peter Dejong/The Associated Press)

Meanwhile, Maltais targets the government's own Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act. Thomson said "the law says the government has to have a plan" to set and meet its emissions targets, making it a more straightforward argument in court.
It got an early boost this summer when the judge decided the case could proceed after the government asked for it to be dismissed. The two sides will now exchange written arguments, Thomson said.
Evolving climate science boosting cases
The government's defence in La Rose relied, in part, on the fact that Canada's emissions form a very small part of global emissions and therefore it alone cannot turn the tide on global warming.
The government's witnesses helped bolster this argument this past week, speaking about the challenges of influencing the global climate, even though Canada is a major fossil fuel producer.

Andrew Leach, an energy and environmental economist at the University of Alberta, testified that even if Canada stopped exporting millions of barrels of oil per day to the U.S., you couldn't assume "those emissions would not occur" because the U.S. could find that oil elsewhere and consume it anyway.

items: Canada can't control climate change on its own, economist tells landmark trial

blocks.text: But those emissions still have a measurable impact, and they have been made clearer through huge improvements in climate science.

In recent years, researchers have been able to attribute specific climate disasters like heat waves and floods to climate change, and link emissions of specific fossil fuel producers to changes in the climate.

"In many situations, people are producing scientific reports from the very governments that they are suing. And, so, it's very difficult to be a lawyer from the government and to challenge the findings of a scientific report prepared by your own client," Thomson said.
The judges at the International Court of Justice as they delivered an advisory opinion on international climate obligations in 2025. (Peter Dejong/The Associated Press)
Camille Martini, a doctoral researcher at Université Laval who studies global climate litigation, said lawsuits abroad have also helped drive the "wave" of cases being filed in Canada.

Martini also pointed to the importance of a legal opinion released by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) last year, which said countries have a legal duty to address climate change under international law.
Later, Canada co-sponsored a non-binding resolution in the UN's General Assembly supporting the ICJ's opinion. The resolution was adopted with a vast majority of countries in favour.

items: No catastrophic financial hit required to fight climate change, scientists say in landmark court case

blocks.text: "The ICJ opinion clarified … It's really binding on states to do the utmost possible based on each state's capabilities," Martini said, meaning countries can't say they don't have to act because their own emissions are too small.
"So, I think now is the time for Canada to face the music."
Lawyers for both sides in the La Rose case will return to court in February, where they will have a week to make their closing statements.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Inayat Singh covers the environment and climate change at CBC News. He is based in Toronto and has previously reported from Winnipeg. Email: inayat.singh@cbc.ca

articles.title: Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
articles.summary: The 21m tree is Oslo’s annual thank you for Britain’s support during World War Two.

blocks.text: Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
Image source, Westminster Council
Karen Scarborough (left) and Anne Lindboe got to work with a two-handled saw
This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.
The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.
Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.
Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.
Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.
"This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The 21m tree has been nicknamed Jolly Cheery

blocks.text: The 21m tree has been nicknamed Jolly Cheery
Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square."
Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.
"The tradition has a powerful history, and its message remains just as relevant today.
"I hope Jolly Cheery spreads warmth and Christmas cheer to everyone who passes by, and reminds us how much it means to be there for one another, especially in difficult times."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Count the rings: Anne Lindboe (left) and Karen Scarborough (right) with a slice of the 75-year-old trunk

blocks.text: Count the rings: Anne Lindboe (left) and Karen Scarborough (right) with a slice of the 75-year-old trunk
For the second year running, the tree was chosen with the help of a social media poll.

Organisers said it would travel by road in Norway and England using only electric and biodiesel vehicles, cutting the journey's carbon footprint by 80%. It will cross the North Sea on a regular cargo ship from the port of Brevik.
Once in London, it will be decorated in the traditional Norwegian style, with 25m strings of festoon lighting fitted with energy-efficient bulbs.

blocks.text: A US federal judge sentenced an Indian national on Friday to 19 years and seven months in prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.
Nikhil G.*, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
"I'm sorry to Mr. Pannun," he said in court. Judge Victor Marrero said he faces deportation to India after serving his sentence.
Prosecutors say an Indian government employee recruited the suspect in 2023. The government employee remains overseas and is not in US custody.
The defendant paid $15,000 (€13,670) to a person he believed was a hitman, who was actually an undercover US agent.
Prosecutors also said the defendant had told that agent the day after Hardeep Singh Nijjar's June 2023 killing in Canada that Nijjar "was also the target," the Associated Press reported.
His lawyer, Isabelle Kirshner, denied he had any role in the Nijjar killing.

"There is no question he was not the brains behind this operation," she said. Canada has separately alleged India arranged Nijjar's killing, and India dismissed that, with both countries expelling diplomats.
India-Canada row over Sikh killing has Punjab on edge
India denies any involvement in the Pannun plot. New Delhi has designated Pannun a terrorist.
Pannun, who leads the group Sikhs for Justice, called Gupta a foot soldier and said outside court: "I'm ready to face India's bullet if that is the price I have to pay."
